### Who runs which tests

Steps 4 and 7 both run tests, and they are not running the same ones.

**The main agent runs the test that is the subject of the change. The
`verifier` runs everything else.** The line does not fall between unit
tests and journeys; it falls on what the change is about. A change to the
pager makes `tests/tui.sh` the focused test and it belongs in the loop, slow
as it is. A change to `tuifmt.c` makes the compiled `tuifmt` test the
focused one, fast as it is, and leaves `tui` and the rest to the `verifier`
— including
the golden recordings, which never pass `-t` and so cannot see that file's
panel formatters at all, whatever else in it they reach.

Step 4's loop cannot be delegated at all. It asks you to watch a test fail
for the expected reason, and a sub-agent reporting that it failed correctly
is exactly the trust that failing run exists to withhold. It is also the
tightest loop in the workflow, where a sub-agent round trip costs minutes
against a `ctest -R` that costs a second.

What the `verifier` owns is everything the loop did not reach: the rest of
`ctest`, the full journey and golden battery, and the configurations the
main agent did not build — Release, `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, whatever the platform
adds. It decides that scope for itself: step 7 gives it the criterion, and
step 8 says the decision is the verifier's own. This says only that it
should not be asked to skip what the main agent happened to run, and that
the main agent should not pre-run the battery to save it the trouble.
Running the suite twice buys nothing and costs the whole of it: a full
`ctest` here is about four minutes per configuration.

**Keep what reaches the main agent's context small.** That is the reason
this split is worth stating, and it is mechanical:

- `ctest --output-on-failure` prints no test output on a pass, and `-R`
  scopes it to the test being worked on — anchor the pattern, since it is a
  regex: `-R tui` picks up `tuifmt` and `journey-tui` with it.
- The shell tests print one line on a pass, so they need no filtering. On
  a failure they print what broke and then dump the screen behind it, in
  that order, so it is the first lines that are worth reading and not the
  last. Redirect to a file and read the head of that rather than piping:
  `tests/tui.sh` has no `PIPE` trap, so a `head` that closes the pipe early
  leaves it holding a live tmux server and an `sst -t` inside it (#128).
- Grep a tmux pane for the string being asserted rather than capturing it
  whole. `capture-pane -p` is twenty-odd lines of screen and a TUI check
  makes many; capture the pane when the grep fails, which is when its
  content is worth reading.

**The mutation proof in step 4 can be delegated**, unlike the loop it
belongs to. Shape decides whether it may be: the loop is iterative and each
failure decides the next edit, which is why you watch it yourself, where the
proof is one shot, asked and answered.

What handing it off buys is context and not time. Nothing here comes near a
sub-agent round trip even when it fails, and a failing run is what a proof is:
a broken `tui.sh` goes past two minutes waiting out its polls, where a round
trip is several. Delegate when the failing run would bury this context
instead, which is a property of the test and worth looking up rather than
guessing — one ordinary break in `tui.sh` printed nineteen panes and four

## Verdict: pass

All three fixes (F1-F3) hold, and the three prose items (P1-P3) are answered. Three new prose observations below, none of them false claims — they are for the pull request body if you disagree with them.

### Scope I chose

`git diff` shows exactly two modified files, no staged and no untracked content: `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md` and `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/instructions.sh`. `instructions.sh` has an mtime of `23:20`, before my previous round's own artifacts (`23:30`-`23:48`), which corroborates your "byte-identical" claim independently of your word for it. So I re-ran only the instructions test (direct and through `ctest`), `shellcheck`, one plain-mode smoke journey, and then spent the round on the claims you listed. No builds, no full battery, no `tui.sh` — nothing compiled changed, and re-running the battery over a docs diff buys nothing.

Two of your figures I did *not* have to take on trust: my previous round left its artifacts in `/tmp`, and they are still there. That is where the F1 and F2 confirmations below come from.

### Findings

**F1 — RESOLVED, and now measured rather than argued.** The 2m04s is exact. `/tmp/brk1-tui.out` was created at `23:31:18.520` (the redirect opening = process start) and `/tmp/brk1-tui.err` last written at `23:33:22.602` — 2m04.1s. "Goes past two minutes" is true of that run.

**F2 — RESOLVED, transcribed correctly, and conservatively.** `/tmp/brk4-tui.err`: 19 occurrences of `--- screen`, 19 `FAIL` lines, 456 lines total. Subtracting the 19 headers and 19 fail lines leaves 418 lines of pane. "Nineteen panes and four hundred lines of them" is right and rounds down.

**F3 — RESOLVED.** Every part of the citation checks out against the files on disk, not a copy: `tests/help.sh:42`, `tests/golden.sh:73`, `tests/tournament.sh:103` each `trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 141' PIPE`; `tests/tui.sh:91-94` has the four traps and no `PIPE`. Issue #128 is open, titled "tests/tui.sh has no PIPE trap, so a closed pipe leaks a tmux server", and its body matches what AGENTS.md attributes to it. Both orphaned `/tmp/sst-tui.*` directories are still present and untouched.

**`-R` regex claim — CONFIRMED exactly.** `ctest -N -R tui` in `build-debug` returns three tests: `tuifmt` (#1), `journey-tui` (#4), `tui` (#7). `ctest -N -R '^tui$'` returns one. `-R` is a regex, and both halves of the sentence are literally what the tool does.

**P3 — the added clause does close it.** `condition_now()` is defined in `tuifmt.c:27`, declared in `sst.h:456`, and called from `setup.c:577` (`newcnd()`), which every plain-mode game runs — so the goldens genuinely do reach into that file, which is what the old sentence over-generalized away. The narrowed claim is true: `fmt_quad_line`, `fmt_status_line`, `cell_class`, `status_class` and `sensors_masked` have no caller outside `tuifmt.c` and `tui.c`, and every `tui.c` path into them is behind `tui_active` — `tui_gameover()` (`tui.c:714-717`) is the one entry point called unguarded from `finish.c`, `events.c` and `sst.c`, and it tests the flag itself. `tests/golden.sh` never passes `-t` (`play()` at line 101 runs `run "$SST"` with no flags). "Cannot see that file's panel formatters at all, whatever else in it they reach" is now exactly right.

**`STANDARDS` — CONFIRMED at 4.** The script's own awk over the flattened file prints `4`; the matches are at `AGENTS.md:213`, `:227`, `:237`, `:471`. The new section adds no fifth statement of the phrase. `sh tests/instructions.sh .` prints `instructions OK (CLAUDE.md 174 bytes, AGENTS.md 28688 bytes)`, exit 0; `ctest -R '^instructions$'` passes in 0.05s; `shellcheck -s sh tests/instructions.sh` is clean.

### New prose observations (not failures)

**P4 — the two minutes is not mostly the polls.** From `/tmp/ctest-debug.log`, a *passing* `tui` on this machine takes 105.43s. The broken run took 124s. So the failing run's excess over a passing one is about 19 seconds, and "a broken `tui.sh` goes past two minutes waiting out its polls" reads as though the polls are what put it past two minutes when a passing run is already at 1m45s. The sentence's load-bearing point — that it stays well under a round trip — is unaffected. Related and outside this diff: `CMakeLists.txt:93` says "the ~11s it takes to pass", which is off by a factor of ten on this machine; that is a candidate for step 9, not for this branch.

**P5 — "even when it fails" is bounded for breaks that change output, not for breaks that hang.** Everything I measured supports it (worst case `tui` at 2m04s; my broken-`tournament` run at `23:44` finished in about a minute). But `tests/tournament.sh` plays 14 seeds each under `timeout 60` (`:110`, `:257`), so a mutation that makes the game hang rather than print something different runs up to 14 minutes standalone, and gets killed at `TIMEOUT 300` under ctest. Low severity: a mutation proof normally changes output. Worth a clause only if you want the sentence airtight.

**P6 — the file does not follow its own new advice one screen earlier.** The first hunk changes the TUI bullet to `ctest --test-dir build -R tuifmt`, unanchored, while the new bullet says to anchor. Harmless today — I confirmed `-R tuifmt` matches exactly one test — but it is the same shape of pattern the new bullet warns about.

for the expected reason, and a sub-agent reporting that it failed correctly
is exactly the trust that failing run exists to withhold. It is also the
tightest loop in the workflow, where a sub-agent round trip costs minutes

content.content:
### Who runs which tests

Steps 4 and 7 both run tests, and they are not running the same ones.

**The main agent runs the test that is the subject of the change. The
`verifier` runs the rest of the battery.** Not everything else: the piped
plain-mode journey above and the 80x24/72x24 TUI check stay with whoever
made the change, since they are how you see your own work. The line does not
fall between unit tests and journeys; it falls on what the change is about.
A change to the pager makes `tests/tui.sh` the focused test and it belongs
in the loop, slow as it is. A change to `tuifmt.c` makes the compiled
`tuifmt` test the focused one, fast as it is, and leaves `tui` and the rest
to the `verifier` — including the golden recordings, which never pass `-t`
and so cannot see that file's panel formatters at all, whatever else in it
they reach.



Step 4's loop cannot be delegated at all, and not because a sub-agent
cannot be trusted with it. Each failure decides the next edit, so the run
and the work are one act: what you would hand over is the whole of the
task, and a report arriving afterwards comes after the moment it was
supposed to inform. It is also the tightest loop in the workflow, where a
sub-agent round trip costs minutes against a `ctest -R` that costs a
second.

What the `verifier` owns is everything the loop did not reach: the rest of
`ctest`, the full journey and golden battery, and the configurations the
main agent did not build — Release, `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, whatever the platform
adds. `verifier.md` does not yet ask for that flag, which is #125; until it
does, say so when invoking the pass. It decides that scope for itself: step
7 gives it the criterion, and step 8 says the decision is the verifier's
own. This says only that it should not be asked to skip what the main agent
happened to run, and that the main agent should not pre-run the battery to
save it the trouble. Running the suite twice buys nothing and costs the
whole of it: a full `ctest` here is about four minutes per configuration.



**Keep what reaches the main agent's context small.** That is the reason
this split is worth stating, and it is mechanical:

- `ctest` prints no test output on a pass at all, and `--output-on-failure`
  costs nothing there while saving the second run a failure would otherwise
  need. `-R` scopes it to the test being worked on — anchor the pattern,
  since it is a regex: `-R tui` picks up `tuifmt` and `journey-tui` with it.
- The shell tests print one line on a pass, so they need no filtering. On a
  failure they print what broke and then dump the evidence behind it — a
  pane, a slice of game output, a diff, depending on the script — in that
  order, so it is the first lines that are worth reading and not the last.
  Redirect to a file and read the head of that rather than piping:
  `tests/tui.sh` has no `PIPE` trap, so a `head` that closes the pipe early
  leaves it holding a live tmux server and an `sst -t` inside it (#128).
- Grep a tmux pane for the string being asserted rather than capturing it
  whole. `capture-pane -p` is twenty-odd lines of screen and a TUI check
  makes many; capture the pane when the grep fails, which is when its
  content is worth reading.

**The mutation proof in step 4 can be delegated**, unlike the loop it
belongs to, and for the reason the loop cannot: it is one shot, asked and
answered, and what comes back is checkable. The break has a name, and step
4 wants that name written down anyway, so a report that does not give it is
visibly incomplete.

Not to one of the three review sub-agents — all of them are read-only by
definition, and this one has to break the game. A general-purpose sub-agent
does it, on a copy outside the repository, which step 4 requires in any
case: no file in the repository is modified.

What handing it off buys is context and not time. Nothing here comes near a
sub-agent round trip even when it fails, and a failing run is what a proof
is: a broken `tui.sh` goes past two minutes, its failed polls waiting out
their timeouts on top of a run that is slow already, where a round trip is
several. Delegate when the failing run would bury this context instead,
which is a property of the test and worth looking up rather than guessing —
one ordinary break in `tui.sh` printed nineteen panes and four hundred lines
of them, `tournament.sh` dumps up to 3000 bytes for every seed that fails,
`golden.sh` a diff per changed journey. Below that, and most proofs are
below it — a `ctest -R '^tuifmt$'` answering in a second, a `help` journey
in eight — running it costs less than handing it over.



When you do hand it off, the sub-agent has to report what it broke precisely
enough for the main agent to write that down, since step 4 wants it in the
commit and in a comment beside the assertion.

### The review sub-agents

## Why it matters

Neither section name has a metacharacter today, so nothing is wrong now:

```
check_section 'Answering a finding' ...
check_section 'Who runs which tests' ...
```

The function is the documented extension point — its own comment says "adding
one means adding a call rather than a second copy of this" — so the next name
is written by someone following that instruction, and nothing warns them. A
heading like `### The 3.x flags` or `### Answering a finding (and when not to)`
matches a different set of lines through `grep` than through `index()`, and the
two halves of the check would then disagree about whether the section exists.
Backslashes are worse: `grep` consumes them and `awk -v` consumes them again.

The failure is silent in the direction that matters — a heading check that

**The mutation proof in step 4 can be delegated**, unlike the loop in the
step it belongs to, and for the reason the loop cannot: it is one shot,
asked and answered, and what comes back is checkable. The break has a name,

give it is visibly incomplete.

Not to one of the three review sub-agents — all of them are read-only by
definition, and a proof has to break something. A general-purpose sub-agent
is the one that can, working on a copy outside the repository, so nothing it
touches is tracked. Step 4 already asks for that copy where the proof runs
the game; ask for it whatever the proof breaks, because a sub-agent editing
the tree you are working in is a surprise nobody needs.

What handing it off buys is context and not time. Nothing here costs more
than a sub-agent round trip, even when it fails, and a failing run is what a
proof is: a broken `tui.sh` goes past two minutes, its failed polls waiting
out their timeouts on top of a run that is slow already, where a round trip
is several. Delegate when the failing run would bury this context instead,
which is a property of the test and worth looking up rather than guessing —
one ordinary break in `tui.sh` printed nineteen panes and four hundred lines
of them, `tournament.sh` dumps up to 3000 bytes for every seed that fails,
`golden.sh` a diff per changed journey. Below that, and most proofs are
below it — a `ctest -R '^tuifmt$'` answering in a second, a `help` journey
in eight — running it costs less than handing it over.

When you do hand it off, the sub-agent has to report what it broke precisely
enough for the main agent to write that down, since step 4 wants it in the
commit and in a comment beside the assertion.

# Verdict: FAIL — one actionable factual finding (Finding 1). Everything mechanical passes.

## Scope I chose, and why

The diff is `AGENTS.md` (prose) plus `tests/instructions.sh`, no C. So no builds, no C static analysis, no plain-mode/TUI journey battery — that would have been ceremony. Note: my `CLAUDE.md` snapshot showed base `fef362c`; the branch is actually on `2f7f06d`. Everything below was read from disk, not from that snapshot.

### Finding 1 — FACTUAL, ACTIONABLE. "No proof here costs more than a sub-agent round trip, even when it fails" has a measured counterexample at 3m05s (`AGENTS.md:399-401`)

A single-line break in `tui_refresh_panels()` — `if (1) return;` at the top of the function — is exactly the proof step 4 asks for (break the game, not the test; break it where the test's expectation does not come from) for any `tui.sh` assertion about the panels. ```

```
  broken:  3m05.8s / 3m05.2s   (1209 lines, 47 FAILs)   ← two runs, deterministic
  passing: 1m45.6s / 1m45.9s   (1 line)                 ← two runs, deterministic
```

Against a round trip the same sentence calls "several" minutes, 3m05s is not below the comparator — it is at or past it. The narrowing from "Nothing here" to "No proof here" removed the full-`ctest` counterexample but not this one, which is the same failure at the same boundary. The illustration under it — "a broken `tui.sh` goes past two minutes" — is literally true of 3m05s but reads as ~2m and is offered as the worst case; the worst case I could construct with an ordinary one-line break is over three minutes and 1209 lines.

Two supporting measurements, both deterministic, that do *not* threaten the claim (failing costs the same as passing for these):

| proof | passing | failing (break: `" Condition     %s"` → `" Condtion     %s"` in `reports.c:354`) |
|---|---|---|
| `tests/tournament.sh` | 1m09.5s | 1m09.6s (3 lines, 1 FAIL) |
| `tests/golden.sh` | 43.5s | 43.4s (89 lines, diff per journey) |
| `ctest -R '^tuifmt$'` | 0.01s | 0.01s |
| `ctest -R '^help$'` | 8.34s | — |

Copy + fresh configure + build is negligible here (1.9s + 1.5s on 24 cores), so it does not add to the proof cost in any material way.

Incidentally: my first two breaks (`Condition` in `reports.c`, then the same in `tuifmt.c`) both left `tui.sh` **green** at 1m45s, which is why I escalated to the panel-refresh break. That is not a coverage gap — `golden`/`tournament` caught the `reports.c` side, the compiled `tuifmt` test caught the `tuifmt.c` side, and `tui.sh:621` says in as many words that it does not assert the panels.

`AGENTS.md:177-178` tells you the proof run for compiled tests is `ctest --test-dir <copy>/build` — unscoped. That is the ~4-minute full battery the narrowing to "No proof" was introduced to exclude. The `-R` advice lives in the "Keep what reaches the main agent's context small" bullet (`AGENTS.md:372`), but the sentence a reader follows *at proof time* is step 4's, and followed literally it produces a proof sitting exactly at the round trip's floor. The narrowing closes the claim's wording without closing the path to the counterexample.

### Finding 3 — PASS, with one seam. The subordinated cost clause

`AGENTS.md:351-353` now reads as subordinate, and "a faster harness would not change it" closes off the "cheap enough round trip permits delegation" reading cleanly. It does not reintroduce time as *the* reason.

The seam: "only adds to it" concedes cost as a genuine additional reason for the loop, while `AGENTS.md:399` says flatly "What handing it off buys is context and not time". Those are about different things (the loop vs the proof), so they do not contradict — but a reader who takes the time-disclaimer as the section's stance will feel it. Not actionable in my judgment.

Also checked: "a `ctest -R` that costs a second" is a restrictive relative clause, and it is true of the case it names (`^tuifmt$` = 0.01s). It does not claim every `-R` run is a second, which is just as well — `-R '^tui$'` is 105s.

### Finding 4 — PASS. "unlike the loop in the step it belongs to" is accurate

Step 4's structure on disk: the five loop bullets at `AGENTS.md:146-150`, "Run that loop yourself" at `152`, the mutation-proof bullets at `161-192` with "This proof, unlike the loop above" at `190`. The loop is properly *in* step 4 (one part of it, not the whole), and it is above the proof, so both the new phrase and step 4's signpost are true and agree. Minor redundancy only: the sentence already opens "The mutation proof in step 4", so "the step it belongs to" re-identifies a step named four words earlier.

- `STANDARDS=4`: verified 4 occurrences, located in steps 6, 7, 8 and the `Answering a finding` section — exactly what `tests/instructions.sh:93-94` claims.
- Pointers to `"Who runs which tests"`: exactly 3, all before the heading — `AGENTS.md:152` and `:190` (both step 4), `:232` (step 7). Matches `tests/instructions.sh:211-220`.
- The comment's claim that step 4's first pointer wraps mid-phrase where the others do not is still true after the reflow (line 152 breaks after "Who runs which").
- Mutations re-proved against the current file: heading rename → FAIL; all three pointers removed with a newline-spanning regex → FAIL; all 6 proper non-empty subsets → pass. The eight-subset property holds.
- Reflow width: the new section maxes at 76 chars, and the rest of `AGENTS.md` already runs to 80/81 (one line at 91), so 76 is in keeping. No trailing whitespace, no CR.

## Other claims in the diff, all verified against files on disk

- `#125` OPEN, "verifier.md builds without -DSST_WERROR=ON, which is what CI uses" — and `.claude/agents/verifier.md:23` indeed asks only for `-Wall -Wextra`. Claim holds.
- `#128` OPEN, "tests/tui.sh has no PIPE trap..." — `tests/tui.sh` has 0 PIPE traps; `tournament.sh` and `golden.sh` have 1 each. Claim holds.
- "`-R tui` picks up `tuifmt` and `journey-tui` with it" — `ctest -N -R tui` lists `tuifmt`, `journey-tui`, `tui`. Holds.
- "`tournament.sh` dumps up to 3000 bytes for every seed that fails" — `DUMPBYTES=3000` at `tests/tournament.sh:90`. Holds.
- "the golden recordings, which never pass `-t`" — zero `-t` occurrences in `tests/golden.sh`. Holds.
- "`ctest` prints no test output on a pass at all" — confirmed.
- "a full `ctest` here is about four minutes per configuration" — not re-run (you said the battery is not owed). Corroborated from components: `tui` 105s + `tournament` 69s + `golden` 43s + `help` 8s = 3m45s for four tests alone, so "about four minutes" is a fair floor with `journey`, `journey-tui`, `eof`, `rules`, `score`, `instructions` still to add.

## Missing coverage

None attributable to this diff. `tests/instructions.sh` covers what is mechanically checkable about the new section (heading exists, something points forward at it), and the mutation record in its comments is accurate. The section's factual claims — timings, issue numbers, which script has which trap — are not testable and were checked by hand above.

## Environment issues

- `cppcheck`, `clang-tidy`, `scan-build`: **not installed**. Not owed for a prose diff, but recorded rather than silently skipped. `shellcheck` 
 is present and `shellcheck -x tests/instructions.sh` is clean (exit 0).
- **Builds not run** — deliberate scoping (no C in the diff), not a pass. If you want them anyway, say so.
- Pre-existing leaked processes, not mine and not in the repo: `sst -t` from earlier sessions' scratchpads still running (pids 1867071 under `scratchpad/mutJ`, 2851060 under `scratchpad/copy`). That is the exact shape `#128` describes. My own runs left nothing behind — `tui.sh` cleaned up its own `-L` socket both times.

## What ran (reproducible)

1. `shellcheck -x tests/instructions.sh` — clean.
2. `./tests/instructions.sh $PWD` ×3 (0.04-0.05s, pass each time) and `ctest --test-dir build-debug -R '^instructions$'` — pass.
3. Mutation re-proof on copies of `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` at `/tmp/vfy`, `/tmp/vfy2`, `/tmp/vs`: heading rename, all-3-pointer removal, and all 6 proper non-empty subsets.
4. Count verification with `awk` (mirroring the test's flattening) and a Python locator mapping each hit to its step/section.
5. Timing measurements on a full tree copy at `/tmp/proofcopy` (fresh `build/`, Debug): `tuifmt`, `help`, `tournament.sh`, `golden.sh`, `tui.sh` — each passing, then each with a deliberate break; `tui.sh` broad break timed twice.
6. Claim verification by reading `.claude/agents/verifier.md`, `tests/tui.sh`, `tests/tournament.sh`, `tests/golden.sh`, `CMakeLists.txt` from disk, and `gh issue view 125 / 128`.

Logs kept at `/tmp/t_*.log`; all scratch copies removed.

Scope I chose: the change is docs-only (`AGENTS.md` + `tests/instructions.sh`, both uncommitted; the branch has no commits of its own — `docs/agents-test-split` is at `2f7f06d`, same as `main`). I still ran the full battery both configurations, because the new prose makes numeric claims about that battery and about `AGENTS.md`'s own checks, and every one of those numbers is measurable. I re-measured every falsifiable number in the new paragraph rather than trusting my prior run, and re-ran the documented mutation proofs for the new `check_section` call from a copy outside the repository.

## Verdict: pass, with three findings

Nothing fails. All three findings are about statements in the diff, not about a broken check.

---

## Finding 1 — actionable, factual. "seven lines" and "one line" are correct, but they are pass-run counts sitting in a sentence about failing runs

Both numbers you asked about are exactly right as stated:

- `ctest --test-dir build -R '^tuifmt$'` on a pass: **7 lines** (ctest 4.2.3, full output including chrome). Confirmed.
- `tests/help.sh <sst>` on a pass: **1 line** (`help OK`). Confirmed — and it is one line for every shell test in the suite, which I checked individually rather than by inference: `eof OK`, `journey OK (3710 bytes)`, `golden OK`, `score OK (27 lines, column 47)`, `instructions OK (...)`, `tournament OK (14 seeds, Debug)`, `tui OK`. Eight for eight, one line each.

The problem is the frame. The sentence before them is "delegate when the failing run would bury this context", and the three examples that follow it are all failing-run volumes — 1209 lines, 3000 bytes per failing seed, a diff per changed journey. "Below that ... a `ctest -R '^tuifmt$'` answering in seven lines, a `help` journey in one" is parallel construction on a list of failure outputs, so "answering" reads as answering a break. Measured, on the copy at `/tmp/sst-copy`:

| proof | pass | fail |
|---|---|---|
| `ctest -R '^tuifmt$' --output-on-failure`, one assertion broken (`status_class` case 8 returns `STAT_GOOD`) | 7 lines | **16 lines** |
| same, broader break (`sensors_masked()` returns 1) — 7 assertions | 7 lines | **34 lines** |
| `tests/help.sh`, CR strip broken at `sst.c:188` | 1 line | **62 lines / 2154 bytes** |

`help.sh` caps each dump at `DUMPBYTES=2048` and has three `dump_if_failed` blocks, so its ceiling is nearer 6 KB than one line.

This does not falsify the paragraph's conclusion — 16, 34 and 62 are all far below 1209, so "there is nothing to bury, so keep it" survives with room to spare. But it is the same species as the four comparators that came before it: a number that is true of one thing, offered in a position where it reads as a number about another. Either qualify them as pass output, or use the failure figures, which make the argument better rather than worse (62 against 1209 is still an order of magnitude).

## Finding 2 — actionable, factual. `-R '^tuifmt$'` reaches one of the two compiled tests, and the bullet says "the compiled ones"

`rules` is the other one — `add_test(NAME rules COMMAND test_rules)` at `CMakeLists.txt:59`, from `tests/test_rules.c` + `rules.c`. `ctest -N -R '^tuifmt$'` returns Total Tests: 1.

The anchoring itself is correct and the finding it answers is fixed: `^tuifmt$` no longer drags in `journey-tui` and `tui` the way bare `tui` does (I confirmed `-R tui` still selects all three, so the warning in "Who runs which tests" is accurate). What is off is the plural. An agent who has just written an assertion in `tests/test_rules.c`, follows the bullet literally, and runs `-R '^tuifmt$'` on the broken copy gets `1/1 Test #1: tuifmt ... Passed` — a green run produced by never having run the test under proof, which is precisely the "the test is blind, or the break was" trap two bullets later, arriving by a third route the bullet itself supplied.

`-R '^(tuifmt|rules)$'` works (`ctest -N` returns both), as does naming `rules` separately. Alternatively, mark `tuifmt` as an example rather than as the set.

## Finding 3 — actionable, factual, pre-existing text inside the sentence the diff edits

The clause the diff amends sits in this sentence, whose opening is unchanged context:

> Every test here takes the binary as an argument, so the run is `tests/tournament.sh <copy>/build/sst Debug`, or `ctest --test-dir <copy>/build -R '^tuifmt$'` for the compiled ones

"Every test here takes the binary as an argument" is false for two of the eleven registered tests. `instructions` and `score` take the source directory — `CMakeLists.txt:122-124` and `131-133` both pass `${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}`, and `sh tests/instructions.sh .` is how you ran the very check under review. The "so" makes it load-bearing: it is the premise from which the two example commands are drawn. Raising it because `code-review` is about to re-read this sentence for the third time and it is now half-new; not because the diff introduced it.

---

## Your question 1: can anything in the new paragraph be false?

I went through it clause by clause.

- **"a proof that runs over three minutes is no cheaper delegated"** — holds, in the one direction it asserts. A sub-agent invocation blocks the parent, so a delegated 3-minute run costs the parent ≥ 3 minutes plus round-trip. It cannot come out cheaper. The single hinge is that blocking property: if a harness ever offered a genuinely detached sub-agent, "no cheaper" would become false. That is a property of the tool, not of this repository, and today it holds. Stating it as "no cheaper" rather than "more expensive" is what keeps it safe — the narrower claim is the one that survives.
- **"one line broken in `tui_refresh_panels()` made `tui.sh` report 47 failures and 1209 lines of panes"** — reproduced exactly, from a fresh copy and a fresh build: `if (1) return;` after the declarations at `tui.c:726`, `tests/tui.sh /tmp/sst-copy/build/sst Debug` → 3m05.3s, **1209 lines, 47 FAILs**, exit 1. Identical to the prior session's numbers; deterministic, not flaky. This is the one number in the paragraph that will drift silently — it is a function of how many checks `tui.sh` currently has and of the 80x24/72x24 pane geometry, so any added TUI check moves it.
- **"`tournament.sh` dumps up to 3000 bytes for every seed that fails"** — true. `DUMPBYTES=3000` at `tests/tournament.sh:90`, `tail -c "$DUMPBYTES"` at line 663, inside the per-seed loop guarded by `if [ "$fails" -ne "$before" ]`.
- **"`golden.sh` a diff per changed journey"** — true. `tests/golden.sh:154-164`, per journey, `cmp` then `diff | head -n "$DIFFLINES"` with `DIFFLINES=40`.
- **"most proofs are below it"** — not falsifiable, and reads as the judgment it is.

So: **nothing in the paragraph is false today.** What can go stale is the count of lines, not the comparison — which is the inversion you were going for, and it worked. The three numbers that can rot are 1209/47 (drifts with `tui.sh`'s check count), 3000 (a constant in `tournament.sh`), and 7/1 (ctest's output format and the shell tests' pass line). All three are looked up rather than reasoned from, which is what the paragraph now tells the reader to do.

Other claims in the new section, all verified:

- "a full `ctest` here is about four minutes per configuration" — **4m11.6s Debug, 4m02.5s Release**, 11/11 passing both.
- "`ctest` prints no test output on a pass at all" — true; `--output-on-failure` over an all-green run is 27 lines of summary and nothing else.
- "`-R tui` picks up `tuifmt` and `journey-tui` with it" — true (plus `tui` itself).
- "the shell tests print one line on a pass" — true, eight for eight.
- "on a failure they print what broke and then dump the evidence behind it ... it is the first lines that are worth reading and not the last" — true; the broken `tui.sh` run opens `FAIL: 80x24: the full-screen display never came up` on line 1, pane from line 2. Same shape in `help.sh` and `tournament.sh`.
- "`tests/tui.sh` has no `PIPE` trap (#128)" — true; every other script has all five traps, `tui.sh` has EXIT/INT/TERM/HUP only. #128 is open and titled to match.
- "the golden recordings, which never pass `-t` and so cannot see that file's panel formatters at all, whatever else in it they reach" — true and precisely hedged. `golden.sh` passes no `-t`; `fmt_quad_line`, `fmt_status_line`, `cell_class`, `status_class` and `sensors_masked` have callers only in `tui.c`, while `condition_now()` is also called from `setup.c:577` — which is exactly what "whatever else in it they reach" covers.
- "`verifier.md` does not yet ask for `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, which is #125" — true; no `SST_WERROR` anywhere in `.claude/agents/`. #125 open, titled to match.
- "all of them are read-only by definition" — true for all three agent files.

## Your question 3 — the `STANDARDS` count and the pointer count

Both right.

- `STANDARDS=4`: the flattened count of `actionable finding, or resolve it explicitly` in the current `AGENTS.md` is **4**. The new section adds no fifth statement of it, so the constant needed no change.
- Pointer count: **3** quoted `"Who runs which tests"` after flattening — `AGENTS.md:152` (step 4, beside the loop), `191` (step 4, beside the mutation-proof bullets), `233` (step 7). All three precede the heading at line 332, which is what the `q < h` ordering test requires. The comment in `instructions.sh` describing this is accurate down to the wrap: line 152 breaks the phrase across `which` / `tests`, the other two do not.

I re-ran the mutation proofs the new comment documents, on a copy of `AGENTS.md` outside the repository:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| heading → `### Who runs the tests` | **FAIL** — "has no '### Who runs which tests' section" |
| all 3 quoted pointers removed (newline-spanning `perl -0`) | **FAIL** — "nothing in AGENTS.md points forward at ..." |
| 2 of 3 removed | passes, correctly — one pointer still sends a reader there |
| line-at-a-time `sed 's/"Who runs which tests"/.../g'` | **passes**, leaving 1 of 3 standing |

The last row is the blind mutation the comment warns about, and it reproduces exactly as described. The comment earning its keep is the point: without it the next person runs that `sed`, sees green, and concludes the check is dead.

Both `check_section` calls fire independently — the `Answering a finding` regression still fails on a renamed heading — so the refactor from inline code to a function lost nothing.

---

## Missing coverage

None for this change. `tests/instructions.sh` covers both halves of the new section (heading and pointer) and the mutation proofs show both halves can fail. The prose in `AGENTS.md` that no test can check — the line counts, the four-minute figure, the 1209 — is checkable by hand and I checked all of it; a test that asserted those numbers would need re-recording on every unrelated edit, so its absence is the right call rather than a gap.

Scope I chose: the change is docs-only (`AGENTS.md` + `tests/instructions.sh`, both uncommitted; the branch has no commits of its own — `docs/agents-test-split` is at `2f7f06d`, same as `main`). I still ran the full battery both configurations, because the new prose makes numeric claims about that battery and about `AGENTS.md`'s own checks, and every one of those numbers is measurable. I re-measured every falsifiable number in the new paragraph rather than trusting my prior run, and re-ran the documented mutation proofs for the new `check_section` call from a copy outside the repository.

## Verdict: pass, with three findings

Nothing fails. All three findings are about statements in the diff, not about a broken check.

---

## Finding 1 — actionable, factual. "seven lines" and "one line" are correct, but they are pass-run counts sitting in a sentence about failing runs

Both numbers you asked about are exactly right as stated:

- `ctest --test-dir build -R '^tuifmt$'` on a pass: **7 lines** (ctest 4.2.3, full output including chrome). Confirmed.
- `tests/help.sh <sst>` on a pass: **1 line** (`help OK`). Confirmed — and it is one line for every shell test in the suite, which I checked individually rather than by inference: `eof OK`, `journey OK (3710 bytes)`, `golden OK`, `score OK (27 lines, column 47)`, `instructions OK (...)`, `tournament OK (14 seeds, Debug)`, `tui OK`. Eight for eight, one line each.

The problem is the frame. The sentence before them is "delegate when the failing run would bury this context", and the three examples that follow it are all failing-run volumes — 1209 lines, 3000 bytes per failing seed, a diff per changed journey. "Below that ... a `ctest -R '^tuifmt$'` answering in seven lines, a `help` journey in one" is parallel construction on a list of failure outputs, so "answering" reads as answering a break. Measured, on the copy at `/tmp/sst-copy`:

| proof | pass | fail |
|---|---|---|
| `ctest -R '^tuifmt$' --output-on-failure`, one assertion broken (`status_class` case 8 returns `STAT_GOOD`) | 7 lines | **16 lines** |
| same, broader break (`sensors_masked()` returns 1) — 7 assertions | 7 lines | **34 lines** |
| `tests/help.sh`, CR strip broken at `sst.c:188` | 1 line | **62 lines / 2154 bytes** |

`help.sh` caps each dump at `DUMPBYTES=2048` and has three `dump_if_failed` blocks, so its ceiling is nearer 6 KB than one line.

This does not falsify the paragraph's conclusion — 16, 34 and 62 are all far below 1209, so "there is nothing to bury, so keep it" survives with room to spare. But it is the same species as the four comparators that came before it: a number that is true of one thing, offered in a position where it reads as a number about another. Either qualify them as pass output, or use the failure figures, which make the argument better rather than worse (62 against 1209 is still an order of magnitude).

## Finding 2 — actionable, factual. `-R '^tuifmt$'` reaches one of the two compiled tests, and the bullet says "the compiled ones"

`rules` is the other one — `add_test(NAME rules COMMAND test_rules)` at `CMakeLists.txt:59`, from `tests/test_rules.c` + `rules.c`. `ctest -N -R '^tuifmt$'` returns Total Tests: 1.

The anchoring itself is correct and the finding it answers is fixed: `^tuifmt$` no longer drags in `journey-tui` and `tui` the way bare `tui` does (I confirmed `-R tui` still selects all three, so the warning in "Who runs which tests" is accurate). What is off is the plural. An agent who has just written an assertion in `tests/test_rules.c`, follows the bullet literally, and runs `-R '^tuifmt$'` on the broken copy gets `1/1 Test #1: tuifmt ... Passed` — a green run produced by never having run the test under proof, which is precisely the "the test is blind, or the break was" trap two bullets later, arriving by a third route the bullet itself supplied.

`-R '^(tuifmt|rules)$'` works (`ctest -N` returns both), as does naming `rules` separately. Alternatively, mark `tuifmt` as an example rather than as the set.

## Finding 3 — actionable, factual, pre-existing text inside the sentence the diff edits

The clause the diff amends sits in this sentence, whose opening is unchanged context:

> Every test here takes the binary as an argument, so the run is `tests/tournament.sh <copy>/build/sst Debug`, or `ctest --test-dir <copy>/build -R '^tuifmt$'` for the compiled ones

"Every test here takes the binary as an argument" is false for two of the eleven registered tests. `instructions` and `score` take the source directory — `CMakeLists.txt:122-124` and `131-133` both pass `${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}`, and `sh tests/instructions.sh .` is how you ran the very check under review. The "so" makes it load-bearing: it is the premise from which the two example commands are drawn. Raising it because `code-review` is about to re-read this sentence for the third time and it is now half-new; not because the diff introduced it.

---

## Your question 1: can anything in the new paragraph be false?

I went through it clause by clause.

- **"a proof that runs over three minutes is no cheaper delegated"** — holds, in the one direction it asserts. A sub-agent invocation blocks the parent, so a delegated 3-minute run costs the parent ≥ 3 minutes plus round-trip. It cannot come out cheaper. The single hinge is that blocking property: if a harness ever offered a genuinely detached sub-agent, "no cheaper" would become false. That is a property of the tool, not of this repository, and today it holds. Stating it as "no cheaper" rather than "more expensive" is what keeps it safe — the narrower claim is the one that survives.
- **"one line broken in `tui_refresh_panels()` made `tui.sh` report 47 failures and 1209 lines of panes"** — reproduced exactly, from a fresh copy and a fresh build: `if (1) return;` after the declarations at `tui.c:726`, `tests/tui.sh /tmp/sst-copy/build/sst Debug` → 3m05.3s, **1209 lines, 47 FAILs**, exit 1. Identical to the prior session's numbers; deterministic, not flaky. This is the one number in the paragraph that will drift silently — it is a function of how many checks `tui.sh` currently has and of the 80x24/72x24 pane geometry, so any added TUI check moves it.
- **"`tournament.sh` dumps up to 3000 bytes for every seed that fails"** — true. `DUMPBYTES=3000` at `tests/tournament.sh:90`, `tail -c "$DUMPBYTES"` at line 663, inside the per-seed loop guarded by `if [ "$fails" -ne "$before" ]`.
- **"`golden.sh` a diff per changed journey"** — true. `tests/golden.sh:154-164`, per journey, `cmp` then `diff | head -n "$DIFFLINES"` with `DIFFLINES=40`.
- **"most proofs are below it"** — not falsifiable, and reads as the judgment it is.

So: **nothing in the paragraph is false today.** What can go stale is the count of lines, not the comparison — which is the inversion you were going for, and it worked. The three numbers that can rot are 1209/47 (drifts with `tui.sh`'s check count), 3000 (a constant in `tournament.sh`), and 7/1 (ctest's output format and the shell tests' pass line). All three are looked up rather than reasoned from, which is what the paragraph now tells the reader to do.

Other claims in the new section, all verified:

- "a full `ctest` here is about four minutes per configuration" — **4m11.6s Debug, 4m02.5s Release**, 11/11 passing both.
- "`ctest` prints no test output on a pass at all" — true; `--output-on-failure` over an all-green run is 27 lines of summary and nothing else.
- "`-R tui` picks up `tuifmt` and `journey-tui` with it" — true (plus `tui` itself).
- "the shell tests print one line on a pass" — true, eight for eight.
- "on a failure they print what broke and then dump the evidence behind it ... it is the first lines that are worth reading and not the last" — true; the broken `tui.sh` run opens `FAIL: 80x24: the full-screen display never came up` on line 1, pane from line 2. Same shape in `help.sh` and `tournament.sh`.
- "`tests/tui.sh` has no `PIPE` trap (#128)" — true; every other script has all five traps, `tui.sh` has EXIT/INT/TERM/HUP only. #128 is open and titled to match.
- "the golden recordings, which never pass `-t` and so cannot see that file's panel formatters at all, whatever else in it they reach" — true and precisely hedged. `golden.sh` passes no `-t`; `fmt_quad_line`, `fmt_status_line`, `cell_class`, `status_class` and `sensors_masked` have callers only in `tui.c`, while `condition_now()` is also called from `setup.c:577` — which is exactly what "whatever else in it they reach" covers.
- "`verifier.md` does not yet ask for `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, which is #125" — true; no `SST_WERROR` anywhere in `.claude/agents/`. #125 open, titled to match.
- "all of them are read-only by definition" — true for all three agent files.

## Your question 3 — the `STANDARDS` count and the pointer count

Both right.

- `STANDARDS=4`: the flattened count of `actionable finding, or resolve it explicitly` in the current `AGENTS.md` is **4**. The new section adds no fifth statement of it, so the constant needed no change.
- Pointer count: **3** quoted `"Who runs which tests"` after flattening — `AGENTS.md:152` (step 4, beside the loop), `191` (step 4, beside the mutation-proof bullets), `233` (step 7). All three precede the heading at line 332, which is what the `q < h` ordering test requires. The comment in `instructions.sh` describing this is accurate down to the wrap: line 152 breaks the phrase across `which` / `tests`, the other two do not.

I re-ran the mutation proofs the new comment documents, on a copy of `AGENTS.md` outside the repository:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| heading → `### Who runs the tests` | **FAIL** — "has no '### Who runs which tests' section" |
| all 3 quoted pointers removed (newline-spanning `perl -0`) | **FAIL** — "nothing in AGENTS.md points forward at ..." |
| 2 of 3 removed | passes, correctly — one pointer still sends a reader there |
| line-at-a-time `sed 's/"Who runs which tests"/.../g'` | **passes**, leaving 1 of 3 standing |

The last row is the blind mutation the comment warns about, and it reproduces exactly as described. The comment earning its keep is the point: without it the next person runs that `sed`, sees green, and concludes the check is dead.

Both `check_section` calls fire independently — the `Answering a finding` regression still fails on a renamed heading — so the refactor from inline code to a function lost nothing.

---

## Missing coverage

None for this change. `tests/instructions.sh` covers both halves of the new section (heading and pointer) and the mutation proofs show both halves can fail. The prose in `AGENTS.md` that no test can check — the line counts, the four-minute figure, the 1209 — is checkable by hand and I checked all of it; a test that asserted those numbers would need re-recording on every unrelated edit, so its absence is the right call rather than a gap.

Reporting the three as a gap rather than a pass, per the standing rule — though for a docs-only change none of them would have had anything to read.

Verdict and findings below. I scoped narrowly, as asked, and say exactly what I ran and what I deliberately did not.

## Verdict: pass

No false or actionable finding. Two prose-imprecision notes for the pull request body.

## What I chose to run, and what I skipped

`git diff main --stat` shows only `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md` and `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/instructions.sh`; no C source, no `CMakeLists.txt`, no fixture. Nothing the compiler or the game sees can have changed, so I did not rebuild Debug/Release, did not rerun the journey or golden battery, and did not run the TUI checks — those passed twice last round on a state whose only difference is this prose. Skipped, not passed.

What I did run: the four questions you asked, plus the test that actually covers this file.

## Q1 — "a few dozen lines" and "sixty": fair

Measured in a fresh copy outside the repository (`/tmp/sst-verify-vol`, configured and built there, since a copied `build/` names the original source dir; removed afterwards).

`ctest --test-dir build -R '^tuifmt$' --output-on-failure` costs exactly **13 lines of framing plus 3 lines per failed assertion**, across four independent breaks:

| break in `tuifmt.c` | failures | lines |
|---|---|---|
| quad header literal `10`→`11` | 1 | 16 |
| `quad[j][row]`→`quad[row][j]` in the `coordfixed` branch | 3 | 22 |
| `goodscan = 0` | 5 | 28 |
| both formatters emptied (`buf[0]=0; return;`) | 27 | 94 |

16 reproduces my prior single-assertion figure exactly, and the fitted 13+3n gives 34 at seven failures — my prior figure, though I did not re-run a seven-failure break this round. "A few dozen lines" covers everything up to about eleven failed assertions; the only thing I could push past it was emptying both formatters wholesale, which is not the single targeted break step 4 asks for, and 94 is still not burying anything against 1209.

`help`: with the `\r` dropped from the strip loop at `sst.c:188`, `sh tests/help.sh <copy>/build/sst` prints **62 lines** — reproducing the prior measurement to the line. The same failure through `ctest` is 74 (12 lines of ctest framing). Worst realistic break I could force — `fopen("sst.doc")` misspelled, so `help` finds nothing — is 4 failures and 102 lines. "In sixty" is fair for the targeted break, and it is measured the same way as the 1209 it is set against, which is also a direct-script number.

**Prose imprecision (PR body, not actionable):** both figures are per-targeted-break, and both scale — `tests/help.sh` dumps up to `DUMPBYTES=2048` per failing block and has three blocks, so a break that fails all of them lands near 100 rather than 60. Nothing in the sentence is wrong; a reader taking it as a ceiling rather than a typical case is off by under 2x, and the conclusion ("nothing to bury") holds at either end.

## Q2 — "Most tests here take the binary as an argument": true and now complete

Eleven registered tests (`ctest -N` returns 11), and the three groups the sentence names account for all eleven:

- **7 take the `sst` binary as their first argument**: `journey`, `journey-tui`, `eof`, `help`, `tui`, `tournament`, `golden`. 7 of 11 is "most".
- **2 take the source directory**: `instructions` and `score`, both `COMMAND .../tests/<name>.sh ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}` — exactly the pair the new sentence names, and "take `<copy>` itself" is the right instruction for them.
- **2 take no argument at all**: `tuifmt` (`COMMAND test_tuifmt`) and `rules` (`COMMAND test_rules`), which is why describing them by how you invoke them (`ctest --test-dir`) rather than by an argument is correct.

The taxonomy is now correct about *arguments*, but the prescribed run form — `tests/tournament.sh <copy>/build/sst Debug`, script path relative to wherever you are, binary pointed at the copy — is wrong for four of the seven binary-taking tests, because they locate the tree independently of the binary:

- `tests/help.sh:27,69` and `tests/golden.sh:56-57` and `tests/tui.sh:40,322` resolve `srcdir` from `dirname -- "$0"`, so the *script's* path decides which `sst.doc` and which `tests/golden/` fixtures are used.
- `tests/journey.sh` runs `$SST` in the caller's cwd; `CMakeLists.txt:66-68` sets `WORKING_DIRECTORY` to the source tree precisely because the in-game `help` reads `sst.doc` from there.

Failure scenario, measured just now. `AGENTS.md:188` tells the reader to take the expectation from an independent source and names `sst.doc` first, so "break `sst.doc` in the copy" is the recommended proof shape. Doing that (`warp drive` → `warp drve` in `<copy>/sst.doc`) and then following the bullet from the original tree:

```
<copy>/tests/help.sh <copy>/build/sst      -> FAIL, exit 1, 65 lines
tests/help.sh <copy>/build/sst             -> "help OK", exit 0
```

"the tightest loop in the workflow, where a sub-agent round trip costs minutes against a `ctest -R` that costs a second" describes the loop in general, and the counterexample is nine lines above it in the same section: `AGENTS.md:343` says a pager change makes `tests/tui.sh` the focused test "and it belongs in the loop, slow as it is". The argument does not depend on it ("the entanglement is the reason, and a faster harness would not change it"), so the minimal fix is one clause: qualify it ("a focused test that is often a `ctest -R` costing a second") or drop the timing and keep the entanglement. I would accept a PR-body resolution here only if it says why the fast case may stand as the rule when the section itself names the slow one.

The bullet at `AGENTS.md:373-374` already recommends the flag, so a back-reference ("with `--output-on-failure`, as above") would close it. Resolvable in the PR body.

New `AGENTS.md` lines run 73-78 columns, inside the file's existing range, and the heading level and section ordering (pointer before heading, as the awk requires) are intact.

`ui-review` skip is correct — neither file is compiled, read by `sst` at runtime, or touches `-DSCORE`/`-DCAPTURE`/`-DCLOAKING`; this is the case `AGENTS.md` names as giving that pass nothing to read. Your other resolutions are reasonable and I do not re-raise them.

I did not reproduce the `tui_refresh_panels()` break behind "47 failures and 1209 lines of panes" — it needs a rebuild plus a ~3-minute tmux run; I took your verifier's measurement, and the shape is consistent with `tests/tui.sh` having no `PIPE` trap and dumping panes per failure (#128, confirmed open and correctly described, as is #125 against `.claude/agents/verifier.md`, which indeed never mentions `SST_WERROR`).

### Verification I did on this exact state

- Full `ctest --test-dir /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/build`: 11/11 pass, 251s wall. This closes the gap left by the verifier's last round not re-running the battery for the final prose edit — `AGENTS.md` is the *input* to the `instructions` test, so that edit was inside its blast radius.

**Should-fix — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md:174-181`: the invocation account is still incomplete, and the missing case produces exactly the green-for-the-wrong-reason proof the bullet exists to prevent.**

```
tests/help.sh <copy>/build/sst             -> "help OK", exit 0
```

**Should-fix — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md:354-356`: the time comparator that has been falsified four times survives here, unqualified, in a paragraph this diff adds.**

"the tightest loop in the workflow, where a sub-agent round trip costs minutes against a `ctest -R` that costs a second" describes the loop in general, and the counterexample is nine lines above it in the same section: `AGENTS.md:343` says a pager change makes `tests/tui.sh` the focused test "and it belongs in the loop, slow as it is". The argument does not depend on it ("the entanglement is the reason, and a faster harness would not change it"), so the minimal fix is one clause: qualify it ("a focused test that is often a `ctest -R` costing a second") or drop the timing and keep the entanglement. I would accept a PR-body resolution here only if it says why the fast case may stand as the rule when the section itself names the slow one.

**Nit — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md:409-411`:** the "few dozen lines" / "sixty" figures hold only with `--output-on-failure`; a bare `ctest -R '^tuifmt$'` prints a ten-line summary and a pointer to `LastTest.log`, which is a different number and a second run. 1. **Delegation paragraph (402-411): yes, that paragraph is now clean** — it disclaims the time axis, every figure in it reproduces, and "most proofs are below it" carries the hedge. The failure mode moved rather than died; see the second should-fix.
2. **Step 4 bullet: no, not complete.** The argument taxonomy is right; the working-directory dimension is missing and is where the blind proof lives. First should-fix.

---

## Answers to your three questions

### 1. Is the rewritten sentence true? Yes — all of it.

- **"for some of them"** — correct, and correctly not "every". Of the 7 registered tests that take the binary (`journey`, `journey-tui`, `eof`, `help`, `tui`, `tournament`, `golden`), exactly 3 have the script deciding which tree is read. The other 4 read nothing from any tree: `journey.sh` has no `srcdir`, no `dirname`, no `sst.doc`, and its scripted input (line 70) never issues `help`; `eof.sh` takes only the binary and runs in a `mktemp -d`; `tournament.sh`'s only `$0` uses are awk field references, and its `sst.doc` mentions are all comments citing the manual for hard-coded expectations. Its "calling for help" (line 123) is the `call` command, not `help` — `sst.c:97` and the dispatch at `sst.c:414` confirm `help` is command 36 and the mayday is `call`.
- **`help` and `tui` find `sst.doc` from their own path** — both true, by different mechanisms. `tests/help.sh:27` sets `srcdir` from `dirname $0/..`, then `:65-69` copies `$srcdir/sst.doc` into the scratch dir the game runs in. `tests/tui.sh:40` sets `srcdir` the same way and `:322` sets `startdir="$srcdir"`, which `start()` passes as tmux's `-c`; the comment at `:318-321` gives the reason, and the script really does exercise it — `help move` at `:421`, `help` at `:530` and `:581`.

- **The distributive split holds both ways.** `golden.sh` never issues `help` (its only "help" is the prose comment at `:289`), so it reads no `sst.doc`; `help.sh` and `tui.sh` read no fixtures. The two halves attach to exactly the tests named.
- **"The two that read the tree instead, `instructions` and `score`, take `.` from in there"** — true. Both default `ROOT="${1:-.}"` (`instructions.sh:20`, `score.sh:42`), and both pass when invoked as `sh tests/<script>.sh .` from the tree root. CMake passes them `${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}` (`CMakeLists.txt:122-134`), which is the same argument in absolute form.
- **"Most tests here take the binary as an argument"** — true: 7 of 11 registered tests, or 7 of the 9 shell tests.
- **"the two compiled ones"** — true: `tuifmt` and `rules` are the only `add_executable` tests (`CMakeLists.txt:51-59`).

**FALSE (actionable)** — `AGENTS.md:176-178`:

> `ctest --test-dir build -R '^(tuifmt|rules)$'` for the two compiled ones — **anchored, or you run the whole battery to prove one of them.**

```
$ ctest --test-dir build-verify-debug -N -R '(tuifmt|rules)'

Total Tests: 2
```

There is a parse that rescues it — "use `-R` at all, or else you run the whole battery" — but the word carrying the conditional is "anchored," not "-R", and the bullet is the one place a reader meets the pattern. Not caused by the clause you removed; it was in the previous state and I missed it. Your call whether it is a fix or a resolution.

Nothing else in the bullet depends on the deleted clause. The enumeration is now exhaustive over the binary-taking tests, so no residual "every test" or `journey`-shaped assumption survives. `CMakeLists.txt:63-64` still carries the wrong comment, correctly filed as **#130** (verified open, title matches) and not contradicted by anything AGENTS.md now says.

   unstaged, and untracked files. Remove accidental or unrelated changes while
   preserving work that belongs to the user. What you drop because it was
   unrelated is often worth filing; see step 9.

6. **Run `ui-review` before verification.** After the main agent completes an
   implementation pass, invoke the `ui-review` sub-agent whenever the change
   can alter what the game shows a player or asks of them. The `ui-review`
   sub-agent must act as an expert in games and CLI games. Fix every
   actionable finding, or resolve it explicitly, before moving on — the
   standard that "Answering a finding" below sets for all three passes.

   on the result: the fixes made for #46 introduced a doubled echo, a
   duplicated question, a line cut mid-word and a cursor left where the
   next keystroke typed over the answer, each of them found by a later
   round rather than by the one that caused it. Read "The review
   sub-agents" after this list for when this pass binds, what to say when
   it does not, and — if you are not Claude Code — how to get any of
   these three passes at all.

7. **Run `verifier` before code review.** Invoke the `verifier` sub-agent to
   run the builds, static checks, tests, and journey coverage appropriate for
   the change. The verifier must report failures, flakes, missing coverage,
   and environment issues. Fix every actionable finding, or resolve it
   explicitly, before starting code review. If a verifier finding requires a
   code change, rerun the verifier after addressing it.

   The battery is the `verifier`'s work and not the main agent's, which
   is what "Who runs which tests" after this list is about.

8. **Run `code-review` before every commit.** Invoke the `code-review`
   sub-agent against the current branch diff and every staged, unstaged, and
   untracked file. The reviewer must act as an expert in the languages and
   frameworks used by this application. Fix every actionable finding, or
   resolve it explicitly, before committing. If review findings cause changes,
   rerun the appropriate tests and the `verifier`, then obtain a fresh
   `code-review` approval for the changed state.

   Tell it which of the passes above ran, whether the last `ui-review`
   round saw the state being committed, and where `ui-review` did not
   run, why. The middle one is what makes the rerun rule in step 6
   auditable: a fix made after that pass reported is a change it never
   saw, and "it ran" is a true answer that hides it.

   The skip itself is the author's judgment about the author's own
   change — unlike the `verifier`'s scope, which the `verifier` decides
   and reports for itself. `code-review` binds on every commit whatever the
   change touched, so it is the pass certain to see the claim, and to be
   able to dispute it while the work can still change. Left to the commit
   and the pull request, the decision reaches a reader only once the work
   is finished, which is disclosure rather than review.

9. **File what you found outside the slice.** Work turns up problems that
   belong to no slice in particular: a defect the change did not cause, a
   test that cannot fail, a comment that is no longer true. Open a GitHub

### The review sub-agents

Steps 6-8 invoke Claude Code sub-agents defined in `.claude/agents/`:
`ui-review`, `verifier` and `code-review`. What matters is not the tool. It
is that the work is judged by a reader who did not write it, and who
reaches its conclusions from the diff rather than from a memory of having
intended something.

Which of the three bind depends on what changed. `code-review` binds on
every commit, without exception — it is the gate step 8 describes.
`verifier` binds as well, with the scope step 7 already gives it: the
checks appropriate for the change, which for a file nothing compiles can
come down to a single test — the sub-agent still runs, even when what it
has to run is one test. `ui-review` binds when the change can alter what
the game shows a player or asks of them. This file, a test's plumbing and
CI configuration usually give it nothing to read; the build system does
the moment it changes what gets compiled in, since `-DSCORE`, `-DCAPTURE`,
`-DCLOAKING` and the `-DDEBUG` that Debug builds add all decide which
commands and messages the game has at all.

When it is unclear whether a change reaches the player, run the pass. A
`ui-review` with nothing to say costs one pass; code that runs while the
game runs reaches the player whether the change meant it to or not, and a
refactor that preserves behavior is exactly where a lost line hides.

Skipping it is a decision, not an omission. Say that it was skipped and
why — to `code-review` when invoking it, per step 8, and in the commit,
the pull request body and the summary of the work. The last three put it
on the record; the first is the one that reaches a reviewer with a
mandate to argue back, and reaches it before there is a commit to argue
about, which is why step 8 asks for it as well. An agent writing that
sentence about a change to the game's own output has skipped the wrong
pass.

An agent that is not Claude Code is bound on the same terms, and cannot
satisfy a pass by reviewing its own work.

- **A reviewer is a fresh session holding the reviewer's instructions, the
  change, and nothing else.** A sub-agent where the harness has them; a
  second non-interactive invocation of your own CLI — `codex exec` and its
  equivalents — where it does not. A new session reading the change cold
  satisfies this. The same session in a later turn does not.

  `.claude/agents/ui-review.md`, `verifier.md` and `code-review.md` are the
  specifications. A per-tool definition should say to read the matching
  file and follow it, and carry only the wiring its own harness needs: the
  name, and that the reviewer reports findings and never edits. Copying the
  text is how three tools come to review three different things, which is
  the whole reason this file exists.

  issue tracker all refer to them by name.

plain-mode journey above and the 80x24/72x24 TUI check stay with whoever

fall between unit tests and journeys; it falls on what the change is about.

in the loop, slow as it is. A change to `tuifmt.c` makes the compiled

and so cannot see that file's panel formatters at all, whatever else in it
they reach.

be trusted with it. Each failure decides the next edit, so the run and the
work are one act: what you would hand over is the whole of the task, and a
report arriving afterwards comes after the moment it was supposed to inform.
The entanglement is the reason, so a faster harness would not change it, and
neither would a focused test cheap enough to look worth handing over.

`ctest`, the full journey and golden battery, and the configurations the
main agent did not build — Release, `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, whatever the platform
adds. It decides that scope for itself: step 7 gives it the criterion, and
step 8 says the decision is the verifier's own. This says only that it
should not be asked to skip what the main agent happened to run, and that
the main agent should not pre-run the battery to save it the trouble.

`ctest` here is about four minutes per configuration. One caveat while it
stands: `verifier.md` does not yet ask for `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, which is
#125, so say so when invoking the pass.

this split is worth stating, and it is mechanical:

  need. `-R` scopes it to the test being worked on — anchor the pattern,
  since it is a regex: `-R tui` picks up `tuifmt` and `journey-tui` with it.

  failure they print what broke and then dump the evidence behind it — a
  pane, a slice of game output, a diff, depending on the script — in that
  order, so it is the first lines that are worth reading and not the last.
  Redirect to a file and read the head of that rather than piping:
  `tests/tui.sh` has no `PIPE` trap, so a `head` that closes the pipe early

asked and answered, and what comes back is checkable. The break has a name,
and step 4 wants that name written down anyway, so a report that does not
give it is visibly incomplete.

definition, and a proof has to break something. A general-purpose sub-agent
is the one that can, working on a copy outside the repository, so nothing it
touches is tracked. Step 4 already asks for that copy where the proof runs
the game; ask for it whatever the proof breaks, because a sub-agent editing
the tree you are working in is a surprise nobody needs.

each other: a proof that runs over three minutes is no cheaper delegated,
where one that prints twelve hundred lines is. So delegate when the failing
run would bury this context, which is a property of the test and worth
looking up rather than guessing — one line broken in `tui_refresh_panels()`
made `tui.sh` report 47 failures and 1209 lines of panes, `tournament.sh`
dumps up to 3000 bytes for every seed that fails, `golden.sh` a diff per
changed journey. Below that, and most proofs are below it — a broken `ctest
-R '^tuifmt$'` reports itself, with `--output-on-failure`, in a few dozen
lines, a broken `help` journey in sixty — there is nothing to bury, so keep
it.

enough for the main agent to write that down, since step 4 wants it in the
commit and in a comment beside the assertion.

Steps 6-8 invoke Claude Code sub-agents defined in `.claude/agents/`:
`ui-review`, `verifier` and `code-review`. What matters is not the tool. It
is that the work is judged by a reader who did not write it, and who
reaches its conclusions from the diff rather than from a memory of having
intended something.

Which of the three bind depends on what changed. `code-review` binds on
every commit, without exception — it is the gate step 8 describes.
`verifier` binds as well, with the scope step 7 already gives it: the
checks appropriate for the change, which for a file nothing compiles can
come down to a single test — the sub-agent still runs, even when what it
has to run is one test. `ui-review` binds when the change can alter what
the game shows a player or asks of them. This file, a test's plumbing and
CI configuration usually give it nothing to read; the build system does
the moment it changes what gets compiled in, since `-DSCORE`, `-DCAPTURE`,

game runs reaches the player whether the change meant it to or not, and a
refactor that preserves behavior is exactly where a lost line hides.

why — to `code-review` when invoking it, per step 8, and in the commit,

mandate to argue back, and reaches it before there is a commit to argue

sentence about a change to the game's own output has skipped the wrong

  name, and that the reviewer reports findings and never edits. Copying the

  the whole reason this file exists.

answer, and silence is neither.

**Resolving explicitly** is for the finding you judge wrong, or right
about something this change is not. Say what you think is true instead,
in the words you would use if you expected to be argued with.

Where it goes depends on whether anything else is going to read the
change. A resolution alters no code, so it triggers no rerun: steps 6,

repeating `code-review` over an unchanged worktree. So put it to the
next pass that runs anyway — step 8 already carries `ui-review` facts

without a change there is no next pass, and the record is the whole
of it.

afterwards is the silence this rule exists to stop.
