   and reports for itself. `code-review` binds on every commit whatever the
   change touched, so it is the pass certain to see the claim, and to be
   able to dispute it while the work can still change. Left to the commit
   and the pull request, the decision reaches a reader only once the work
   is finished, which is disclosure rather than review.

9. **File what you found outside the slice.** Work turns up problems that
   belong to no slice in particular: a defect the change did not cause, a
   test that cannot fail, a comment that is no longer true. Open a GitHub
   issue for each as you find it, without waiting to be asked — a finding
   that lives only in a session summary is a finding nobody will act on.
   Standing here at step 9 makes this the last check that nothing was left
   unfiled, not the moment to begin. The main agent files them; the review
   sub-agents only report.

   - Search the open issues first. If it is already filed, add what you
     learned to that issue instead of opening a second one.
   - File a real defect — anything that would mislead a player or a
     maintainer — and a coverage gap, meaning a test that cannot fail or
     that asserts less than it appears to. Leave style preferences and
     speculative ideas out; they belong in the pull request body. When it
     is genuinely unclear, file it: a wrong issue costs one close.
   - **Do not fix it in this slice.** An unrelated fix buried in an
     unrelated diff is how both the fix and the finding go unreviewed. Fix
     it here only if it belongs to the slice.
   - That is not license to file what steps 3, 4 and 6-8 require you to
     fix. A premise the slice rests on is corrected under step 3, not
     deferred; a test of your own that cannot fail is fixed under step 4. A
     `ui-review`, `verifier` or `code-review` finding about *this* change is
     resolved here; filing it is not resolving it. What gets filed is what
     those reviews turn up about code the change did not touch, and
     whatever you meet while reading for some other purpose.
   - Give the issue what the next person needs: what is wrong, why it
     matters, where it was found, and how to see it, citing `sst.doc` or a
     file and line where one applies.
   - Where the work depends on the unfixed behavior, name the issue in a
     comment beside it. Write that comment as part of the implementation,
     so it reaches the reviewer rather than arriving after approval.
   - Say which issues were filed, in the pull request body and in the
     summary of the work — in the summary alone when there is no pull
     request. An agent that cannot open issues says so plainly and lists
     the findings in the same places, marked as unfiled, so a human can
     file them. Silence is the one outcome this step exists to prevent.

10. **Commit once the passes are answered.** Commit only after verification
    and code review are complete, with every finding answered — a finding
    resolved rather than fixed needs no fresh approval, which is why this
    does not say "after approval". Use Conventional Commits:

    ```text
    <type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>
    ```

    Keep the subject at 72 characters or fewer, describe why in the body when
    useful, and do not combine unrelated work.

11. **Create pull requests from the reviewed state.**
    - Confirm that local verification remains valid.
    - Rerun `code-review` only if the reviewed state changed after the
      pre-commit review. A changed state includes code, tests,
      documentation, generated files, conflict resolution, or any other
      staged, unstaged, or untracked content.
    - Do not repeat code review when the already-reviewed diff and
      worktree remain unchanged. The `verifier` follows the same
      condition: what makes either pass run again is a changed state. A
      finding answered by argument alone leaves both passes nothing they
      have not already seen, and a round of findings answered by edits
      takes one rerun over the result rather than one per finding.
    - Push and create the pull request only after local verification and
      any required code review are complete.
    - Open a normal, ready-for-review pull request by default. Do not
      open draft pull requests unless the user explicitly asks for a
      draft.

12. **Merge only clean, passing pull requests.** Merge only after GitHub
    reports a clean merge state and every configured check passes. Never
    bypass a failing or pending required check. Self-merges are allowed
    when these conditions are met.
    Use squash merge for short-lived development branches to keep `main`
    linear, then delete the merged branch.

### Who runs which tests

Steps 4 and 7 both run tests, and they are not running the same ones.

**The main agent runs the test that is the subject of the change. The
`verifier` runs the rest of the battery.** Not everything else: the piped
plain-mode journey above and the 80x24/72x24 TUI check stay with whoever
made the change, since they are how you see your own work. The line does not
fall between unit tests and journeys; it falls on what the change is about.
A change to the pager makes `tests/tui.sh` the focused test and it belongs
in the loop, slow as it is. A change to `tuifmt.c` makes the compiled
`tuifmt` test the focused one, fast as it is, and leaves `tui` and the rest
to the `verifier` — including the golden recordings, which never pass `-t`
and so cannot see that file's panel formatters at all, whatever else in it
they reach.

Step 4's loop cannot be delegated at all, and not because a sub-agent cannot
be trusted with it. Each failure decides the next edit, so the run and the
work are one act: what you would hand over is the whole of the task, and a
report arriving afterwards comes after the moment it was supposed to inform.
The entanglement is the reason, so a faster harness would not change it, and
neither would a focused test cheap enough to look worth handing over.

What the `verifier` owns is everything the loop did not reach: the rest of
`ctest`, the full journey and golden battery, and the configurations the
main agent did not build — Release, `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, whatever the platform
adds. It decides that scope for itself: step 7 gives it the criterion, and
step 8 says the decision is the verifier's own. This says only that it
should not be asked to skip what the main agent happened to run, and that
the main agent should not pre-run the battery to save it the trouble.
Running the suite twice buys nothing and costs the whole of it: a full
`ctest` here is about four minutes per configuration. One caveat while it
stands: `verifier.md` does not yet ask for `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, which is
#125, so say so when invoking the pass.

**Keep what reaches the main agent's context small.** That is the reason
this split is worth stating, and it is mechanical:

- `ctest` prints no test output on a pass at all, and `--output-on-failure`
  costs nothing there while saving the second run a failure would otherwise
  need. `-R` scopes it to the test being worked on — anchor the pattern,
  since it is a regex: `-R tui` picks up `tuifmt` and `journey-tui` with it.
- The shell tests print one line on a pass, so they need no filtering. On a
  failure they print what broke and then dump the evidence behind it — a
  pane, a slice of game output, a diff, depending on the script — in that
  order, so it is the first lines that are worth reading and not the last.
  Redirect to a file and read the head of that rather than piping:
  `tests/tui.sh` has no `PIPE` trap, so a `head` that closes the pipe early
  leaves it holding a live tmux server and an `sst -t` inside it (#128).
- Grep a tmux pane for the string being asserted rather than capturing it
  whole. `capture-pane -p` is twenty-odd lines of screen and a TUI check
  makes many; capture the pane when the grep fails, which is when its
  content is worth reading.

**The mutation proof in step 4 can be delegated**, unlike the loop in the
step it belongs to, and for the reason the loop cannot: it is one shot,
asked and answered, and what comes back is checkable. The break has a name,
and step 4 wants that name written down anyway, so a report that does not
give it is visibly incomplete.

Not to one of the three review sub-agents — all of them are read-only by
definition, and a proof has to break something. A general-purpose sub-agent
is the one that can, working on a copy outside the repository, so nothing it
touches is tracked. Step 4 already asks for that copy where the proof runs
the game; ask for it whatever the proof breaks, because a sub-agent editing
the tree you are working in is a surprise nobody needs.

What handing it off buys is context and not time, and the two do not track
each other: a proof that runs over three minutes is no cheaper delegated,
where one that prints twelve hundred lines is. So delegate when the failing
run would bury this context, which is a property of the test and worth
looking up rather than guessing — one line broken in `tui_refresh_panels()`
made `tui.sh` report 47 failures and 1209 lines of panes, `tournament.sh`
dumps up to 3000 bytes for every seed that fails, `golden.sh` a diff per
changed journey. Below that, and most proofs are below it — a broken `ctest
-R '^tuifmt$'` reports itself, with `--output-on-failure`, in a few dozen
lines, a broken `help` journey in sixty — there is nothing to bury, so keep
it.

When you do hand it off, the sub-agent has to report what it broke precisely
enough for the main agent to write that down, since step 4 wants it in the
commit and in a comment beside the assertion.

### The review sub-agents

Steps 6-8 invoke Claude Code sub-agents defined in `.claude/agents/`:
`ui-review`, `verifier` and `code-review`. What matters is not the tool. It
is that the work is judged by a reader who did not write it, and who
reaches its conclusions from the diff rather than from a memory of having
intended something.

Which of the three bind depends on what changed. `code-review` binds on
every commit, without exception — it is the gate step 8 describes.
`verifier` binds as well, with the scope step 7 already gives it: the
checks appropriate for the change, which for a file nothing compiles can
come down to a single test — the sub-agent still runs, even when what it
has to run is one test. `ui-review` binds when the change can alter what
the game shows a player or asks of them. This file, a test's plumbing and
CI configuration usually give it nothing to read; the build system does
the moment it changes what gets compiled in, since `-DSCORE`, `-DCAPTURE`,
`-DCLOAKING` and the `-DDEBUG` that Debug builds add all decide which
commands and messages the game has at all.

When it is unclear whether a change reaches the player, run the pass. A
`ui-review` with nothing to say costs one pass; code that runs while the
game runs reaches the player whether the change meant it to or not, and a
refactor that preserves behavior is exactly where a lost line hides.

Skipping it is a decision, not an omission. Say that it was skipped and
why — to `code-review` when invoking it, per step 8, and in the commit,
the pull request body and the summary of the work. The last three put it
on the record; the first is the one that reaches a reviewer with a
mandate to argue back, and reaches it before there is a commit to argue
about, which is why step 8 asks for it as well. An agent writing that
sentence about a change to the game's own output has skipped the wrong
pass.

An agent that is not Claude Code is bound on the same terms, and cannot
satisfy a pass by reviewing its own work.

- **A reviewer is a fresh session holding the reviewer's instructions, the
  change, and nothing else.** A sub-agent where the harness has them; a
  second non-interactive invocation of your own CLI — `codex exec` and its
  equivalents — where it does not. A new session reading the change cold
  satisfies this. The same session in a later turn does not.
- **Point at the definitions here rather than restating them.**
  `.claude/agents/ui-review.md`, `verifier.md` and `code-review.md` are the
  specifications. A per-tool definition should say to read the matching
  file and follow it, and carry only the wiring its own harness needs: the
  name, and that the reviewer reports findings and never edits. Copying the
  text is how three tools come to review three different things, which is
  the whole reason this file exists.
- **Keep the three names.** The workflow above, the commit history and the
  issue tracker all refer to them by name.
- **Land the definition as its own change,** on its own branch and commit,
  before the work it will review — not beside a feature, which step 10
  forbids and step 3 argues against. It belongs in the repository rather
  than in someone's local configuration for the same reason this file
  does: the next session in that tool then inherits a reviewer instead of
  improvising one, and an improvised reviewer drifts. That commit is also
  the one place self-review cannot be avoided, since step 8 cannot be
  satisfied by the commit that creates the reviewer. Say so in the commit,
  and disclose it as below.
- **Confirm the harness actually loads what you wrote.** A definition in a
  directory the tool never reads is inert, and from the outside it looks
  exactly like a step that was carried out.
- **Self-review is the last resort, not the default.** Taking it means
  saying which mechanism you looked for and why it was not there — or, for
  the commit that creates the reviewer, that it did not yet exist. Say it
  in the pull request body and in the summary of the work — in the summary
  alone when there is no pull request. A reviewer who shares the author's
  memory of what was intended is the one thing this section exists to prevent.

### Answering a finding

Steps 6, 7 and 8 hold their passes to one standard, in the same words:
fix every actionable finding, or resolve it explicitly. Two ways to
answer, and silence is neither.

**Fixing** is the ordinary one, and most findings deserve it.

**Resolving explicitly** is for the finding you judge wrong, or right
about something this change is not. Say what you think is true instead,
in the words you would use if you expected to be argued with.

Where it goes depends on whether anything else is going to read the
change. A resolution alters no code, so it triggers no rerun: steps 6,
7 and 8 each condition theirs on a change, and step 11 forbids
repeating `code-review` over an unchanged worktree. So put it to the
next pass that runs anyway — step 8 already carries `ui-review` facts
into `code-review`, and a `verifier` finding you resolve is one
`code-review` should hear about. For a `code-review` finding resolved
without a change there is no next pass, and the record is the whole
of it.

Either way it goes in the pull request body and in the summary of the
work — in the summary alone when there is no pull request, on the same
terms steps 3 and 9 already set. A resolution nobody can find
afterwards is the silence this rule exists to stop.

What does not count: fixing something adjacent and calling the finding
handled, agreeing and then forgetting, or "I disagree" with no reason
under it. Filing an issue does not answer a finding about *this*
change — step 9 is explicit that filing is not resolving — but a
finding about code the change did not touch is answered by filing it
and saying so, which is step 9 working as intended rather than an
exception to it.

Sixteen verifier rounds. It **failed the change five times**, every failure a measurably false claim I'd written:

- The `2>&1 | head` I originally recommended **kills `tests/tui.sh` mid-run and leaks a live tmux server** — that script alone has no `PIPE` trap. Two orphaned servers from earlier sessions were already sitting on your machine. Filed as #128 and cited inline in the text.
- "No single test runs longer than two minutes" — a broken `tui_refresh_panels()` measures 3m05s.
- I claimed `journey` reads `sst.doc`. It never issues `help`. I'd taken that from `CMakeLists.txt:63-64`, whose comment says so — a wrong comment that had propagated into my draft before the verifier caught it (#130).

The time-based argument for delegating was falsified five times across successive narrowings. It's deleted rather than narrowed again.

## Issues filed

#125 (`verifier.md` builds without `-DSST_WERROR=ON`), #126, #127, #128, #129, #130 — plus measured `tui` timings added to the existing #101.

## One thing worth your judgment

Step 4 now also carries four corrections the reviews found in the bullet this change had to edit — including that the prescribed proof run was **from outside the copy**, where `help`, `tui` and `golden` resolve `sst.doc` and their fixtures from the script's own path. `code-review` measured it: with `warp drive` broken in the copy's `sst.doc`, `tests/help.sh <copy>/build/sst` returns `help OK`. That's a green mutation proof for exactly the reason the bullet's stale-`build/` warning exists — so the procedure has been quietly capable of blind proofs. It's fixed, but it's the kind of thing you may want to know had been sitting there.

`ui-review` was skipped (nothing compiled, nothing the game prints); disclosed to `code-review`, which agreed three times.

content.text:
31 open. Ten of them I filed today. Grouped by what they actually are:

## The one to do first

**#128 — `tests/tui.sh` has no `PIPE` trap.** One line, matching the three sibling scripts. It's leaking right now: two orphaned tmux servers with live `sst -t` processes are on your machine from Aug 8 and Aug 10, and `AGENTS.md` now has to tell readers "redirect to a file rather than pipe" as a workaround for it.

## Player-facing TUI defects

| | |
|---|---|
| **#117** | A resize loses an ended prompt once you've part-typed the answer — and my comment on it corrects the body: it loses **both** the question and the answer. This is the one where an unseen `y` makes a typed `N` mean yes, and it can end a game. |
| #118 | A height shrink can let a restored ended prompt overwrite live conversation |
| #114 | `restore_curline()`'s height-only branch anchors to the bottom of the window |
| #94, #95 | Below 14 rows there's no prompt at all; at 14–15 the pager has no lines to page |
| #90 | Columns outside every window keep text from a wider terminal |

**#117/#118/#114 are all one function.** They'd be better as one careful rewrite of `restore_curline()` than three patches — #117's own fix sketch says the comparison needs to model two rows rather than one, which is what #118 and #114 are also about.

## `tests/instructions.sh` — seven issues on one 240-line script

#105 (prefix-matched headings), #109 (a quoted pointer with no heading), #110 (no floor under "Answering a finding"), #126 (accepts one pointer where its message claims two), #129 (regex on one side, literal on the other), #65 (workflow numbering), #98 (unvalidated command output compared as numbers).

Several explicitly point at each other — #129 says to do it with #105 and #126; #126 says it may belong to #65. **All seven want the same thing: per-step attribution, so the check can say "step 4 no longer points at this" instead of "nothing does."** Doing them one at a time will mean touching that script seven times and probably fighting the same awk each time.

## Comments that state something false

#101 (`tui` timeout says ~11s, measures 55–106s), #127 (`tournament` timing wrong in all three claims), #130 (`journey`'s `WORKING_DIRECTORY` cites an `sst.doc` read the test never makes). Three tiny fixes in two files — one sweep. Worth doing because #130 already propagated a false claim into my AGENTS.md draft before the verifier caught it.

## Documentation reach and accuracy

#120 (most of `sst.doc` unreachable from in-game `help` — the manual's scoring table and the whole `-t` section included), #122 (README's resize section over-promises then contradicts itself), #121 (MODIFICATIONS is 125 lines against a 47–67 band).

## Coverage gaps

#123 (nothing ties the 15/14/13-row thresholds to behaviour), #115, #89, #76, #106 (no shellcheck in CI or ctest).

## Agent infrastructure

#125 (`verifier.md` doesn't pass `-DSST_WERROR=ON` — I'm currently telling each verifier invocation to do it by hand), #81, #84, #85, #86, #93.

---

**Recommendation:** #128 today, then the `restore_curline()` cluster as one slice, then the `instructions.sh` seven as one rewrite. Four are tagged *good first issue* if you want to hand something off: #65, #76, #81, #84.

# every capture comes back empty and the game gets blamed for it.
tm() { tmux -f /dev/null -L "$socket" "$@"; }

# tmux leaves the socket file behind when the server exits, so a suite
# that ran often would slowly fill the directory with dead ones. This is
# where tmux puts them on both Linux and macOS: $TMUX_TMPDIR if it is
# set, /tmp otherwise.
cleanup() {
	tm kill-server 2>/dev/null
	rm -f "${TMUX_TMPDIR:-/tmp}/tmux-$(id -u)/$socket"
}

# The saved-game cases write a .trk file, which the game puts in the
# directory it is playing in. That must not be the source tree.
work=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/sst-tui.XXXXXX")
if [ -z "${work:-}" ] || [ ! -d "$work" ]; then
	echo "FAIL: could not create a temporary directory" >&2
	exit 1
fi

finish() { cleanup; rm -rf "$work"; }
trap 'finish' EXIT
trap 'finish; exit 130' INT
trap 'finish; exit 143' TERM
trap 'finish; exit 129' HUP

The issue says "the other **three** shell tests that dump on failure all set a
fifth". It is five, and the right frame is not "the ones that dump" but "the
ones that create anything to clean up":

```
tests/eof.sh          EXIT INT TERM HUP PIPE
tests/golden.sh       EXIT INT TERM HUP PIPE
tests/help.sh         EXIT INT TERM HUP PIPE
tests/journey.sh      EXIT INT TERM HUP PIPE
tests/tournament.sh   EXIT INT TERM HUP PIPE
tests/tui.sh          EXIT INT TERM HUP
tests/instructions.sh  (none)
tests/score.sh         (none)
```

`instructions.sh` and `score.sh` set no traps because they only read files and
make no temporary state. So `tui.sh` is not one of four that mostly agree — it
is the **only** script in the suite that takes a trap set at all and is missing
one of them, and it is the one whose cleanup does more than `rm -rf`.

## Reproduced, and the mechanism confirmed

The leak is real and it does not need a failing run. `tui.sh` writes nothing
until `printf 'tui OK\n'` at the very end, so a consumer that has already
exited SIGPIPEs that final write, before the `EXIT` trap:

```

```

added, the same command leaves no socket, no process and no directory.

Mechanism, isolated so the fix is not being credited for something else — two
stubs differing only in the trap, each writing after the reader is gone:

```

without PIPE trap: script exit 141, cleanup did NOT run
```

That is the whole of it: the shell dies of the signal and the `EXIT` trap
never runs.

Worth recording that my first attempt at that stub was blind — it printed

"cleaned up". A `sleep` before the writes is what makes the difference
observable.

failed. It is: `cleanup` runs `tm kill-server 2>/dev/null` and `rm -f`, neither
of which writes to stdout, and the verified run above shows it completing.

`EXIT` on the way out — which is harmless here and is the same shape the other

## Verdict: pass

The change does what it claims. I reproduced the leak and its absence independently, and everything in the battery is green in both configurations. Four notes below, two of them about the accuracy of the new comment; none of them blocks.

## What ran

Diff inspected first: `git diff main` is exactly two files, `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md` (5 lines) and `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/tui.sh` (8 added lines), no mode change, nothing staged or untracked. No C source, so the builds are a regression check rather than the subject.

| Check | Command | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Debug build | `cmake -S . -B build-verify-debug -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug -DSST_WERROR=ON && cmake --build build-verify-debug -j` | clean, no warnings (`-DSST_WERROR=ON` per the note about #125) |
| Release build | same with `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` | clean, no warnings |
| Full battery, Debug | `ctest --test-dir build-verify-debug --output-on-failure` | 11/11 passed, 251.9 s (`tui` 105.7 s) |
| Full battery, Release | `ctest --test-dir build-verify-release --output-on-failure` | 11/11 passed, 242.3 s (`tui` 96.4 s) |
| Static, shell | `shellcheck -s sh tests/*.sh` and on both before/after copies | clean, rc=0, no new findings |
| Plain-mode journey | `printf 'regular\nshort\nnovice\nxyz\nsrscan\nquit\nn\n' \| build-verify-{debug,release}/sst` | rc=0 both, srscan renders, clean exit, zero CRs in output |
| Piped-ctest workflow | `ctest --test-dir build-verify-debug -R '^tui$' --output-on-failure 2>&1 \| head -2` | no leaked socket, dir or process |

Reproduction was done on copies at `/tmp/verif128/{before,after}` (whole tree minus `.git` and `build*`; `before/tests/tui.sh` from `git show main:tests/tui.sh`, `after` byte-identical to the worktree, differing only in the trap and comment). Each variant run twice, driven through a fifo whose reader (`head -n 0`) exits at once, which is `2>&1 | head -n 0` with the script's own status observable. Everything I created I removed; the two pre-existing orphans `/tmp/sst-tui.474IVX` and `/tmp/sst-tui.6Q7RWJ` with their live servers `sst-tui-1866986` and `sst-tui-2851038` I did not touch, and they are still there.

## Reproduction: confirmed, deterministic

Pre-fix, both runs (sockets `sst-tui-256849`, `sst-tui-272659`):

```
262945 tmux -f /dev/null -L sst-tui-256849 new-session -d -x 70 -y 20 -s tui ... sst -t ; sleep 30
262946 bash -c '.../build-verify-debug/sst' -t ; sleep 30
262951 .../build-verify-debug/sst -t
srw-rw---- /tmp/tmux-1000/sst-tui-256849
/tmp/sst-tui.Eg14Dg/sav.trk
```

Post-fix, both runs: `script exit=141`, `leaked_sockets=[] leaked_dirs=[] leaked_procs=0`. Deterministic on both sides, no flake in four runs.

Two details worth adding to yours. The leaked server is the `70x20` one, the last `start` in the file — on a *passing* run the only write to stdout is the final `printf 'tui OK\n'`, so the SIGPIPE arrives at the very end and strands whatever session was last created; on a failing run it arrives earlier, as #128 describes. And I separated signal death from `exit`, which the shell's `$?` cannot: `os.waitpid` on the two stubs gives `without.sh: returncode=-13 (killed by signal 13)` against `with.sh: returncode=141 (exited 141)`. So "the shell dies of the signal" is literally true, not just status-141-shaped.

## `exit 141` and the double cleanup: right, and the same shape as the siblings

- Trap table, all seven other scripts: `eof`, `golden`, `help`, `journey`, `tournament` each set EXIT/INT/TERM/HUP/PIPE with `exit 141`; `instructions.sh` and `score.sh` set none. Your premise correction is right and the issue body's "other three" is wrong.
- `exit 141` matches `128 + SIGPIPE`, and matches all five siblings verbatim in shape.
- Double cleanup is harmless and status-preserving. `finish` twice: second `tm kill-server` returns 1 with its message already sent to `/dev/null` (measured: `pass1 rc=0`, `pass2 rc=1`), `rm -f`/`rm -rf` are idempotent. A `finish` whose last command *fails* still leaves the script at 141 in both dash and bash — I checked with a stub whose `finish` is `false`. cat > "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/i7.md" <<'EOF'
Six of the eight scripts in `tests/` set traps, and until #128 they did not all
set the same ones. `tests/tui.sh` was missing `PIPE`, which left a private tmux
server and a running game behind whenever its output was piped into something
that exits early. The other five had it; nothing noticed for as long as that
was true, and nothing would notice if it happened again.

```
tests/eof.sh          EXIT INT TERM HUP PIPE
tests/golden.sh       EXIT INT TERM HUP PIPE
tests/help.sh         EXIT INT TERM HUP PIPE
tests/journey.sh      EXIT INT TERM HUP PIPE
tests/tournament.sh   EXIT INT TERM HUP PIPE
tests/tui.sh          EXIT INT TERM HUP PIPE   (PIPE added by #128)
tests/instructions.sh  (none -- reads files only)
tests/score.sh         (none -- reads files only)
```

## Why it matters

The trap set is the only thing standing between a killed test run and a leaked
process, and every one of these scripts creates something that outlives it if
the cleanup is skipped: a `mktemp -d` in five of them, and in `tui.sh` a tmux
server with `sst -t` inside it.

It is also a defect that hides. The two orphans #128 was filed from had been
running for thirteen hours and two and a half days before anyone looked, under
per-run socket names nobody would think to grep for. A script added later with
four traps instead of five would go the same way.

`AGENTS.md`'s "Who runs which tests" section now tells readers to pipe test
output through `head` to keep it out of a context, which is exactly the
invocation that trips a missing `PIPE` trap. The advice and the guard belong
together.

## How to see it

```sh
for f in tests/*.sh; do
    printf '%-24s %s\n' "$f" "$(grep '^trap' "$f" | sed 's/.*[; ]\([A-Z]*\)$/\1/' | tr '\n' ' ')"
done
```

Delete the `PIPE` line from any of the six and the whole suite still passes.

## Fix sketch

A static check with precedent in `tests/instructions.sh`, which already asserts
structural properties of files rather than behaviour: for every `tests/*.sh`
that sets any trap, assert it sets all five signals and that each handler calls
the same cleanup. Cheap, and it can be broken to prove it — deleting one `trap`
line should fail it.

The behavioural alternative — run a script into a closed pipe and assert
nothing is left — costs about 100 seconds for `tui.sh` alone and needs tmux, so
it is not worth it for a property this static one covers.

Worth deciding at the same time whether `instructions.sh` and `score.sh` should
be exempt by name or by "creates no temporary state", since a future edit that
gives one of them a `mktemp -d` should not silently fall outside the check.

## Provenance

Reported by the `verifier` while verifying #128 as missing coverage: with that
fix in place, nothing in the suite fails if the trap is deleted again. Filed
rather than fixed there, per AGENTS.md step 9 — it is a property of all six
scripts, not of the one the fix touched.
EOF

fix(tests): trap PIPE in tui.sh so a closed pipe cannot leak a server

whose cleanup does more than remove a directory: it kills a private

broke and drop the pane behind it, grep -q to ask whether anything did
-- left the server up, the game up, the socket in place and the work
directory behind. Under a per-run socket name, sst-tui-<pid>, that
nobody would think to look for: the two orphans that prompted the
issue had been running thirteen hours and two and a half days before
anyone noticed.

It needs no failing run. The script writes nothing until the final
`printf 'tui OK'`, so a reader that has already gone takes the signal
at the very last write, after the whole suite has passed.

closed pipe. It writes nothing there on tmux 3.6, measured with the
server present and absent, so that is hardening rather than a fix --

git log --show-signature -1 --format='%G?' 2>&1 | head -1
cat > "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/pr3.md" <<'EOF'
Closes #128.

`tests/tui.sh` set `EXIT`, `INT`, `TERM` and `HUP` but not `PIPE`. Every other
script here that sets traps at all sets all five, and this is the one whose
cleanup does more than remove a directory — it kills a private tmux server
with a game running inside it.

So piping the output anywhere that can exit early — `head` to keep what broke
and drop the pane behind it, `grep -q` to ask whether anything did — left the
server up, the game up, the socket in place and the work directory behind,
under a per-run socket name (`sst-tui-<pid>`) nobody would think to look for.
The two orphans that prompted the issue had been running thirteen hours and
two and a half days before anyone noticed.

It needs no failing run: the script writes nothing until the final
`printf 'tui OK\n'`, so a reader that has already gone takes the signal at the
very last write, after the whole suite has passed.

## Also in the diff

- **`cleanup()`'s stdout is redirected.** It was pointed at the same closed
  pipe. `kill-server` writes nothing there on tmux 3.6 — measured with the
  server present and absent — so this is hardening rather than a fix, but a
  cleanup reached from a `PIPE` trap should not depend on the state of stdout
  at all. Raised by `code-review`.
- **`AGENTS.md`.** The "Keep what reaches the main agent's context small"
  bullet told readers to redirect to a file rather than pipe, and named this
  missing trap as the reason, citing #128. That goes false here, so the bullet
  returns to the plain advice.

## Premise correction (step 3)

#128 said "the other **three** shell tests that dump on failure all set a
fifth". It is five, and the line is not which scripts dump but which create
anything to clean up — `instructions.sh` and `score.sh` set no traps because
they only read files. So `tui.sh` was the only script in the suite that took a
trap set at all and was missing one of them, which makes the case stronger
rather than weaker. [Posted on the issue.](https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/128#issuecomment-5255324848)

## How it was proved (step 4)

No automated test — the behavioural one costs a 100-second run inside a
4-minute battery. Proof is by reproduction:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `sh tests/tui.sh ./build/sst Debug 2>&1 \| head -n 0` | socket `sst-tui-214645`, live `tmux`, live `sst -t`, a `/tmp/sst-tui.*` dir | nothing |
| `sh tests/tui.sh ./build/sst Debug` | `tui OK` | `tui OK` |

Mechanism isolated in two stubs differing only in the trap: without it dash
dies of signal 13 with the `EXIT` trap unrun; with it the script exits 141 and
cleanup runs. **bash runs that trap before re-raising**, so this leaks where
`/bin/sh` is dash — this machine and the Ubuntu runners — and not where it is
bash.

**My first stub was blind**, and how is worth recording: it wrote before `head`
had exited, so no `SIGPIPE` was ever delivered and both variants appeared to
clean up. A `sleep` before the writes is what makes the difference observable.

The `verifier` reproduced all of it independently rather than accepting my
account, including leaking a server from an out-of-repo copy of the tree
holding `HEAD`'s version of the script — so the check is known to be able to
fail.

## Review passes

`verifier`: three runs, all pass. The first raised two accuracy errors in my
comment — it claimed "every other script here already had" the trap (wrong for
the two that set no traps) and stated dash's behaviour as if it were every
shell's. The third ran the full battery in both configurations *because the
changed file is itself a ctest-registered test*: 11/11 each.

`code-review`: two runs, approve then approve. The first raised the
`cleanup()` stdout hardening and a wrap nit; the second found nothing.

`ui-review` **skipped**: a test's signal handling and a paragraph of
`AGENTS.md`, neither compiled nor read by the game at runtime, no feature-flag
surface, nothing that changes what the game shows a player or asks of them.
Disclosed to `code-review`, which agreed both times.

## Resolved rather than fixed

- `2>&1 | head` yields `head`'s status, not the script's, and POSIX `sh` has no
  `PIPESTATUS`. A reader takes the verdict off the text (`tui OK` versus
  `FAIL:`) rather than `$?`, and a truncated failing run still exits non-zero.
- Nothing in the suite exercises the fix: deleting the trap again would leave
  all 11 tests green. That is #132, and it is why this ships without a test of
  its own.
- On a macOS runner, where `/bin/sh` is bash, the pre-change script would not
  have leaked at all. The comment says so.

## Issues filed (step 9)

- #132 — nothing checks that the test scripts agree on their trap sets

## Left alone

The two pre-existing orphans (`/tmp/sst-tui.474IVX`, `/tmp/sst-tui.6Q7RWJ`
and their live servers) are untouched. They are evidence on #128, they are not
this session's, and `AGENTS.md` forbids the blunt cleanup that would take them.
They can be cleared by socket name now that the leak is closed.
EOF
git push -u origin fix/tui-pipe-trap 2>&1 | tail -2
gh pr create --title "fix(tests): trap PIPE in tui.sh so a closed pipe cannot leak a server" --body-file "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/pr3.md"

content.text:
**#128 is closed.** `main` is at `8fbb4db`, all four CI jobs green.

## The fix

`trap 'finish; exit 141' PIPE` in `tests/tui.sh`, matching the five sibling scripts. Plus `cleanup()`'s stdout redirected — it was pointed at the same closed pipe, which is the one remaining way the handler could have died on the signal it exists to catch.

Two things came out of it worth knowing:

**It needed no failing run.** The script writes nothing until the final `printf 'tui OK'`, so *any* consumer that has already exited SIGPIPEs that last write — after the whole suite has passed. That's a wider blast radius than the issue described.

**The leak is dash-specific.** bash runs the EXIT trap before re-raising; dash doesn't. `/bin/sh` here and on the Ubuntu runners is dash, so this machine is the leaking configuration and macOS never was.

## On the proof

My first stub was blind — it wrote before `head` had exited, so no SIGPIPE was ever delivered and both variants appeared to clean up. A `sleep` before the writes is what made it observable. The `verifier` then reproduced the whole thing separately, including leaking a server from an out-of-repo copy holding `HEAD`'s script, so the check is known to be able to fail rather than assumed to be.

Also corrected on the issue: it said three sibling scripts set `PIPE`. It's five — the line isn't which scripts dump on failure but which create anything to clean up.

## Filed

**#132** — nothing checks that the test scripts agree on their trap sets, so deleting this line again would leave all 11 tests green. That's why the fix ships without a test of its own.

## One thing left for you

The two pre-existing orphans are still running — 13 hours and 2½ days old:

```
/tmp/sst-tui.474IVX   socket sst-tui-1866986
/tmp/sst-tui.6Q7RWJ   socket sst-tui-2851038
```

I left them deliberately: they were evidence on #128 and they aren't this session's to kill. Now that the leak is closed you can clear them by socket name — `tmux -L sst-tui-1866986 kill-server` and the same for the other, then `rm -rf` the two directories. Say the word and I'll do it.

content.content:
=========== #117 ===========
A resize does not restore an ended prompt once the answer is part typed
#112 restores a prompt that ended its own line — `prout` appends the newline, so
`curline` is empty by the time the reader waits, and the question used to vanish
on a resize. The fix keeps the finished line and puts it back.

It deliberately does **not** do so once the player has begun typing.

## Why

An ended prompt and its part-typed answer occupy two rows, with curses' padding
between them. `restore_curline()` compares against a single joined string, and
spanning that boundary went wrong twice in review:

- Leaving the answer out of the comparison meant the tail test never fired, so a
  drag reprinted the question **once per width step** — copies stacking up the
  window, which is the exact failure `restore_curline()`'s comparison exists to
  prevent.
- Padding the answer back to the row boundary fixed that and turned a one-row
  height shrink (80x24 → 80x23) into a **second copy** instead.

Both were found by `ui-review`; the second was my fix for the first.

## What happens now

With an answer part typed, an ended prompt is left alone on a resize — the
behaviour before #112. The answer itself is still restored by the ordinary
`curline` path, so the player can see what they have typed; the question above
it is at worst truncated, exactly as it was.

That is milder than either failure above, which is why it is the state that
ships. It is still worth fixing.

## Fix sketch

The comparison needs to model two rows rather than one. Either:

- build `want` as prompt, padding, answer and verify it against what
  `mvwinnstr()` actually returns for the prompt row — the padding assumption is
  what broke on the height shrink, and it should be measured rather than
  computed; or
- compare the two parts separately, locating the prompt row first and the answer
  row under it, which avoids the padding question entirely.

The rewrite branch needs the same care: `rows` currently adds the prompt and
answer lengths together, and for an ended line they do not share a row.
=========== #118 ===========
A height shrink can let a restored ended prompt overwrite live conversation
`restore_curline()`'s erase branch assumes the rows at the bottom of the message
window are the stump of the line it is restoring. Where a height shrink clipped
an ended prompt away instead, they are not, and the reprint lands on real
conversation.

## How to see it

```
./build/sst -t tournament 7 short novice pw
rest 5000   -> "Are you sure?"   answer n
rest 5000   -> "Are you sure?"   answer n
rest 5000   -> "Are you sure?"   leave it pending
resize 80x24 -> 78x20
```

Gives:

```
 COMMAND> rest 5000
 Are you sure?
 Are you sure?
```

The `n` that answered the middle ask has been overwritten by the restored
question, so the transcript reads as though the game asked twice in a row.

## Scope

Not a regression, and better than what it replaces. `main` at the same shape
shows the last line as `n` with no question at all and the reader silently
waiting — which is #112 itself. So this is a net improvement that leaves a
smaller artifact behind.

## Fix sketch

The branch computes how many rows the stump occupies from the old width and
erases back from the last non-blank row. That is right when the bottom rows
really are the stump. Where the shrink discarded the prompt rather than
truncating it, the rows it erases are older conversation.

Distinguishing them needs something the branch does not currently have: whether
the line being restored was on screen at all before the resize. The search
above already answers that — it fell through, which is why the branch was
reached — but it does not distinguish "found nothing because the line was
=========== #114 ===========
restore_curline()'s height-only branch anchors to the bottom of the window
`restore_curline()` in `tui.c` has two branches for placing the line it rebuilds.

The `oldmsgw > 0` branch — the terminal's width changed — anchors to the last row
with anything on it, and its comment explains why that matters:

> Anchored to the last row with anything on it, not to the bottom of the window.
> They are the same once the conversation has filled it, and different for the
> whole setup conversation and after every `clearscreen()` -- there the live line
> sits mid-window, and writing at the bottom left the stump above it with blank
> rows in between.

The `else` branch — width unchanged, so only the height moved — does not:

```c
wscrl(wmsg, 1);
wmove(wmsg, maxy - 1, 0);
```

The same argument applies to it. Where the conversation has not filled the
window, this puts the rebuilt line at the bottom with blank rows above it,
instead of directly under the conversation.

## Why it is not fixed already

It cannot be reached to be tested. Getting into that branch needs the pending
pair — the game's part-written line plus the answer being typed — to be longer
than the whole message window, since a pair that fits is found intact by the
search above and the branch is never entered. The longest pair the game can
produce is a prompt plus the 126-character input buffer, about 135 characters.
The smallest message window with two rows to scroll is wider than that.

So the defect is real by inspection and unreachable by construction, at least at
every terminal size the display accepts.

A fix would be the same expression the other branch uses, but it interacts with
the `wscrl()` on the line above — after a scroll the row that `last` named holds
different content — so it is not a copy-paste, and there is no way to observe
whether it is right.

## What would make it testable

Either a larger input buffer (`tui.c`'s own comment at the top of
`restore_curline()` says the 512/2048 buffers there want revisiting if the input
buffer grows), or a message window smaller than two rows of the longest pair,

content.text:
## Verdict

**Needs changes.** The core of #117 is genuinely fixed and reads well: at 80x24, 72x24, and every drag step between them a one-character answer to `Are you sure?` comes back with its question, once each, on the right rows, with the cursor sitting immediately after the echoed answer — so the screen no longer lies about what the reader is holding, and the `Ctrl-U` recovery `sst.doc` prescribes now matches what the player sees. But the read-back still models the answer as exactly one row, and an answer that wraps past one row reintroduces precisely the failure the old gate existed to prevent: on every height-only resize the question **and** its answer are stamped out again, stacking three copies up the message window at plain 80x24 and pushing live conversation off the top. That is reachable by a player who answers a yes/no question in a sentence, so it should be fixed before this lands.

## Findings

**1. Blocker — a wrapping answer duplicates the whole exchange on every height resize.** `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c:468`

```c
int start = r - wantlen / width - (ended ? 1 : 0);
```

`wantlen` is now the question alone, and the `- 1` allows the answer exactly one row. When the typed answer wraps, the last non-blank row is the answer's *second* row, the join starts on the answer's *first* row, the question is never in `joined`, `strstr` misses, and the write path runs. On a height-only change that path takes the `oldmsgw == 0` branch, which scrolls and writes without erasing — so each step adds a copy. Width changes are safe only because that branch erases the stump first.

Reproduced at 80x24, `tournament 7 short novice pw`, `rest 5000`, then typing `yes I am quite sure about this captain and I would like to rest for a very long while indeed` (91 chars, no Enter), then 24→23→24→23→24:

```
 Are you sure?
 yes I am quite sure about this captain and I would like to rest for a very lon
 Are you sure?
 yes I am quite sure about this captain and I would like to rest for a very lon
 g while indeed

 Are you sure?
 yes I am quite sure about this captain and I would like to rest for a very lon
 g while indeed
```

Three questions, two of them with a truncated answer under them, the `COMMAND> rest 5000` line pushed off. The same at 72x24 (70 columns of `y`, drag 24→23→22→21→…→24) — the count climbs 1, 2, 3. On `HEAD` the same journey restores nothing at all, so this is a regression relative to the current behaviour, and it is the exact shape ("stood eight copies of it up the window") the comments above this code forbid. Input still works — the cursor lands on the live copy and `Ctrl-U` clears it — but the player is looking at what appears to be three pending questions.

Suggestion: make the step-back count the answer's rows, not one row, e.g.

```c
int alen = (ended && pending_answer != NULL) ? (int)strlen(pending_answer) : 0;
int arows = ended ? (alen > 0 ? (alen - 1) / width + 1 : 1) : 0;
int start = r - wantlen / width - arows;
```

The tail test needs no change: `joined` is a contiguous concatenation of full rows, so the existing `strncmp(joined + skip, pending_answer, alen)` already spans the row boundary correctly once the rows are actually in `joined`. Worth re-checking the `wscrl` / `r > maxy - 1` arithmetic below it with a two-row answer after the fix.

**2. Nit — a question that exactly fills its row gets a blank line before its answer, and then duplicates on the way back.** `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c:638` (`if (ended && maxy > 1) waddch(wmsg, '\n');`)

When `waddstr` fills the row exactly, curses has already wrapped the cursor to the next row and the `'\n'` moves it down a second time, so the answer lands two rows below the question. The next resize then fails to find the pair for the same reason as finding 1. Reproduced at 48x24 with the `   remaining time.  Are you sure this is wise?"` prompt (46 chars, `msgw = COLS - 2 = 46`): a blank row appears between question and answer at 48, and returning to 80x24 leaves the question printed twice. Only reachable below the documented 72-column minimum — no prompt in the game is exactly 70 or 78 characters — hence a nit, but the guard is cheap: skip the newline when `linelen % width == 0`.

**3. Nit — the new test cannot see finding 1.** `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/tui.sh:1385-1412`

The #117 block sends a single `y`, so the "question exactly once, answer on the row below" assertion only ever exercises the one-row-answer case; the whole file passes (`tui OK`) against the build that stacks three copies. The file's own comment at `tui.c:610` already names "a wrapping answer" as the shape that exposes this class of bug. Suggest a second pass through the same drag with an answer longer than the message window (70+ chars at 72 columns), asserting the question exactly once there too.

**4. Nit (player-invisible, but it will mislead the next reader) — stale comment.** `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c:571`: *"Defensive, not live: the #117 gate means pending_answer here is NULL or empty."* The gate is gone, so that padding branch is live now — and it is what computes the erase height for the exact-fill case in finding 2.

**Positives worth keeping:** the one-row message window (80x14) renders the pair as `Are you sure? y` on its single row with the cursor after the `y`; a wrapping *question* with a short answer (46x24 → 80x24) restores intact and once; the unanswered ended prompt, the part-typed `COMMAND>` line, and `[HIT SPACE BAR TO CONTINUE]` all still behave as before; `Ctrl-U` then `n` answers no and returns to `COMMAND>`; the residual `yN`-answers-yes behaviour is now visible on screen as `yn`, which is the honest outcome the issue argues for.

## What I exercised

Built `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug`; drove `./build/sst -t` under tmux on a private socket (`-L revsst`, `-f /dev/null`), plus a pristine `HEAD` build in `/tmp` on a second private socket for before/after comparison. Both servers killed, no bare `kill-server`.

- `rest 5000` → `y` (unsent), then 80x24 → each of 80x23, 80x14, 20x8, 72x24 and back; checked question count, answer row, and `cursor_x/cursor_y` at each.
- Slow width drags 80→72→120 and height drags 24→8→24, one step at a time, counting the question at every step.
- Same journeys with a wrapping answer (70 `y`s at 72 wide; a 91-character sentence at 80 wide) — finding 1.
- Wrapping *question* via `warp 1` / `move 1 8 8` (`…are you sure this is wise?"`) at widths 46, 47, 48, 49, 50, 52, each in a fresh session — finding 2.
- Two-row and one-row message windows (80x15, 80x14) and large terminals (120x40, 200x50, 200x24).
- Regression paths: unanswered ended prompt across four resizes; part-typed `COMMAND> srsca` across three resizes; `[HIT SPACE BAR TO CONTINUE]` across four resizes; `Ctrl-U` → `n` → back to `COMMAND>`.
- Plain mode byte-identical to `HEAD`: `printf 'tournament 7\nshort\nnovice\nsrscan\nrest 5000\ny\nn\n' | ./build/sst` diffed against the pristine build.
- Full `tests/tui.sh ./build/sst Debug` — passes (`tui OK`), which is itself finding 3.
- Read `sst.doc:1570-1595` (the resize paragraph); its advice remains accurate, and the fix makes its "if both are on screen, carry on" branch actually reachable at ordinary sizes.

input.prompt:
Second review round on the uncommitted change in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek (`git diff main` — `tui.c` and `tests/tui.sh`). It fixes #117: `restore_curline()` refused to restore a prompt that ended its own line once the player had begun typing an answer.

A previous round found one blocker and three nits. All four are addressed.

**Blocker — a wrapping answer duplicated the whole exchange on every height resize.** You were right: `start = r - wantlen / width - (ended ? 1 : 0)` allowed the answer exactly one row, so with a two-row answer the question fell outside the joined rows, the search missed, and the height-only branch scrolled and wrote without erasing. The step-back now counts the answer's rows:

```c
int alen = ended && pending_answer != NULL ? (int)strlen(pending_answer) : 0;
int arows = alen > 0 ? (alen - 1) / width + 1 : 0;
int start = r - wantlen / width - arows;
```

That alone did **not** fix it, which is worth knowing: a height shrink cuts the answer's last row, so the on-screen answer is a truncated copy of `pending_answer` and `strncmp` over the full length could never match. The tail test now compares as much of the answer as is on screen — a prefix — and anything else in those columns still fails it and is reported as an overwrite.

Your reproduction now holds at 1 question per step: `rest 5000`, then the 91-character sentence, then 24→23→24→23→24 gives one question each time and the answer comes back whole across its two rows.

**Nit 2 — a question that exactly fills its row got a blank line before its answer.** Guarded, and in three places rather than one: the write path's `waddch('\n')`, the tail test's padding boundary, and the cursor placement all rounded up unconditionally, so a question ending exactly on a row boundary would have skipped a whole row in each. Only the first was visible; the other two are the same arithmetic in the comparison.

**Nit 3 — the test could not see the blocker.** There is now a separate block, `a wrapping answer to an ended prompt`, that types a 90-character answer at 80 columns and drags 23/24/23/24, asserting the question is on screen exactly once at each step. It failed on the first step before the fix and passes after; the whole file passes.

**Nit 4 — the stale comment** about the `#117` gate making a branch defensive is rewritten, since the gate is gone and that branch is live.

What I want: whether the blocker is really gone at every shape rather than just the one you reported, whether the prefix comparison has opened any way for something drawn over the line to be mistaken for our own answer, whether the exact-fill guard is right (you reproduced that at 48x24, below the documented minimum), and whether anything else about what the player sees has moved. Please drive it rather than reading the diff. Report findings; do not edit files.

content.text:
## Verdict

Acceptable as-is on the behaviour it set out to fix. I drove the change rather than read it, across ~90 resize steps at 12 different widths and 15 heights with answer lengths 0/1/30/40/60/90/125, and could not make the question duplicate once — including a 24-step randomised soak at supported sizes. The answer comes back whole at every supported shape I tried, the cursor lands after it, and the reader's buffer always matched what was on screen. The exact-fill guard is right in all three places. The one thing that should change before this lands is documentation: `sst.doc` and `README.md` still describe the limitation this change removes, and they tell the player to throw away an answer that is now intact — including at the self-destruct password. One nit found at 16 columns, and one test-coverage nit that belongs on an issue already open.

## Answers to the four questions

**Is the blocker gone at every shape?** Yes, as far as I could push it. Question count stayed at exactly 1 through: 80x24↔23↔24↔23↔24 with a 91-char answer (your repro); 80x24→22→21→20→19→18→24; width drags 80→79→78→77→76; corner drags 75x23 / 74x22 / 73x21 / 72x24; 72-column minimum with height drags to 22, 20, 16, 15, 14 and back; narrow sweep 40/30/20/16/12 columns and back to 80; and 24 random shapes in 72-101 x 16-29. The answer's own text also survived: 91 b's back across two rows at 80x24, 41 b's back whole after a round trip through 12 columns.

**Has the prefix comparison opened a way to mistake something else for our own answer?** Not in a way a player can be hurt by. A false accept needs the on-screen text at the answer's columns to *equal* the answer for its whole visible length and then be blank to the end of the joined rows — I checked the two near-misses by hand and both correctly fall through to the write path (old answer `n` under a pending `no`, and old answer `no` under a pending `n`). The one false accept I did construct is benign by construction: two identical `Are you sure?` asks, the older one answered `n`, the newer pending with `n`, shrunk to 80x21 — the cursor parks on the *older* pair and the echo redraws `n` over `n`. Because `want` is the question itself, a false match can only happen against text identical to what would be drawn there, so the screen stays truthful; typing `Q` appended to give `nQ`, which is exactly what the reader held.

**Is the exact-fill guard right?** Yes in all three places, exercised at 16x24 where msgw is 14 and `Are you sure? ` fills the row exactly. Write path: no blank row between question and answer. Tail test: 24↔23 drags with both a 1-char and a 20-char (wrapping) answer give one question and the whole answer. Erase arithmetic: 16→20→24→16→40→80 leaves no stump and does not eat `COMMAND> rest` on the row above. Worth recording that no supported width can reach the guard — the longest ended prompt in the game is about 55 characters, so `linelen % width == 0` needs width ≤ 55, i.e. under 57 columns.

**Has anything else the player sees moved?** Plain mode is byte-identical on a deterministic journey. `tests/tui.sh` passes. Pauses, setup prompts, the command prompt, backspace and Ctrl-U across a resize, and the self-destruct password prompt all behave. Two things moved for the better and are not regressions: at 72x14/80x14 the pair now reads ` Are you sure? y` on the single row instead of unrelated stale conversation, and the #118 shape (78x20) now restores correctly *when an answer is pending*, where main showed a bare `n` with the reader waiting invisibly.

## Findings

**1. should-fix — the manual now describes the bug as current behaviour. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.doc:1553-1556` and `:1582-1584`; `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/README.md:53-56`.**
`sst.doc` says "Resizing can still cost you a question you had begun to answer, leaving the game waiting unseen for the rest of your answer" and "A question you had already begun answering may not come back at all"; README says "The one gap left is a question you have already started answering: that one is left exactly as it was before". Verify the uncommitted change in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek (`git diff main`). It fixes issue #117 — read the issue and both of its comments, which carry measurements.

**Four files.** `tui.c` is the fix; `tests/tui.sh` is the test; `sst.doc` and `README.md` are in the diff because the fix makes what they said false.

**The defect.** `restore_curline()` refused to restore a prompt that ended its own line once the player had begun typing an answer. On a one-row height shrink `wresize()` cuts the answer's row and keeps the question's, so the screen read as a clean unanswered question while the reader still held the typed `y` — a typed `N` then submits `yN`, `ja()` takes the `y`, and I reproduced `rest 5000` running and the game ending on it.

**The fix**, which is the second of the two options the issue's fix sketch offers — model two rows rather than one:
- `want` is the question alone for an ended line. A single joined string can only match all or none of the pair, and a height shrink leaves half of it on screen.
- the read-back steps back over every row the answer takes, not one
- the tail test steps over curses' padding and then over as much of the answer as is on screen — a prefix, since the shrink truncates it — before asking whether the rest is blank
- three places that rounded up to the next row boundary unconditionally are guarded for a question that fills its row exactly

**Step 4.** Two rounds of failing-first, both against `tests/tui.sh`:
1. The existing #117 block asserted only "never more than one question", which tolerates zero. It now asserts the question exactly once **and** the typed answer on the row below. It failed at all three drag sizes (20x8, 80x14, 80x23) before the fix.
2. `ui-review` then found a blocker my first attempt introduced — a wrapping answer duplicated the whole exchange on every height step, three copies up the window. I added a block, `a wrapping answer to an ended prompt`, that types 90 characters at 80 columns and drags 23/24/23/24 asserting one question per step. It failed on the first step, and it failed again after my first fix for it, which is what turned up the truncated-answer case.

**`ui-review` ran three times.** Round 1: one blocker, three nits. Round 2: acceptable, one should-fix (the docs described the bug as current behaviour and told players to discard an answer that is now intact — including the self-destruct password). Round 3: acceptable, one should-fix in `README.md` (a rewritten paragraph left "that one" without its antecedent, so the Ctrl-U warning read as blanket advice) plus two nits, all taken. The residual case is measured: at 72 columns with a 90-character answer, 72x16 and above restores both, 72x15 keeps the answer and loses the question, 72x14 leaves a fragment.

**Issues commented rather than fixed:** #94 (a 16-column exact-fill garbles the question, below the documented minimum in both dimensions), #115 (the new test block asserts the question but not the wrapping answer, the gap that issue already owns), #122 (one of its three items has flipped now that this is fixed).

What I want from you:

- the full battery in both configurations, since `tui.c` is game source and this is the display code
- whether the fix can be broken — please mutate it yourself rather than trusting my two failing-first runs, and tell me which mutants the suite catches and which it does not
- whether anything in `restore_curline()` is now unreachable, or reachable only in a way the comments no longer describe
- whether `sst.doc`'s added lines are CRLF and under 70 columns, and whether the manual and `README.md` now agree with the game and with each other
- plain mode unchanged

Note per `AGENTS.md`: `verifier.md` does not yet ask for `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, which is #125.

Report failures, flakes, missing coverage and environment issues. Do not fix anything.

**Verdict: pass.** Every check I ran came back green; the findings below are missing coverage and stale comments, not failures.

## What ran

Repo: `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek`, branch `main`, four modified files uncommitted (`tui.c`, `tests/tui.sh`, `sst.doc`, `README.md`); nothing staged, nothing untracked. Worktree is exactly as I found it — I reconfigured `build-debug`/`build-release` and restored their `SST_WERROR=ON` cache afterwards; all other work was in `/tmp` copies.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `cmake -S . -B build-debug -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug && cmake --build build-debug` | clean, 0 warnings |
| same for Release | clean, 0 warnings |
| both build types again with `-DSST_WERROR=ON` (per #125, since `verifier.md` does not yet ask for it) | clean |
| `ctest --test-dir build-debug --output-on-failure` | 11/11 passed, 257 s |
| `ctest --test-dir build-release --output-on-failure` | 11/11 passed, 248 s |
| `tests/tui.sh ./build-debug/sst Debug` standalone rerun | passed |
| `tests/tui.sh` in a clean `/tmp` copy of the worktree | passed |
| `shellcheck -s sh tests/tui.sh` vs `main`'s copy | both clean, no new findings |
| `gcc -Wshadow -Wconversion -Wsign-conversion` on `tui.c` vs `main`'s `tui.c` | one new warning (below) |
| plain mode vs a build of `main` (`git archive main`): setup/scan/quit journey, tournament journey through `rest 5000`→`y`, `TERM=dumb -t` fallback | byte-identical; `golden` passing in both configs is the byte-for-byte check |

Four `tui.sh` runs, no flakes. Every failure I saw was deterministic (each mutant below failed identically on its named assertion).

## Mutation testing of the fix

Eleven mutants, each in a fresh `/tmp` copy with its own `build/`, run as `tests/tui.sh <copy>/build/sst Debug`. **Killed 8, survived 3.**

Killed — the suite really does test the fix:

| Mutant | Caught by |
|---|---|
| restore the removed `pending_answer` gate (full revert) | `ended: after 20x8 / 80x14 / 80x23 …` — all three sizes |
| `arows = 0` (never step back over the answer's rows) | 80x23 block + wrapping block |
| `arows` capped at 1 | `wrapped answer: at 80x24 …` only |
| disable the answer-prefix skip in the tail test | 80x23 block + wrapping block |
| demand the whole answer instead of the on-screen prefix | `wrapped answer: at 80x23 …` |
| `want` = question+answer joined (failed attempt 1) | 80x23 + wrapping |
| `want` = question+padding+answer (failed attempt 2) | 80x23 + wrapping |

Both of your failing-first rounds reproduce independently: mutant 1 fails at all three drag sizes, and the wrapping block is the *only* thing that catches the one-row `arows` cap.

Survived:

- **The three exact-fill guards are untested.** Removing `i % width != 0` at `tui.c:554`, `linelen % width != 0` at `tui.c:669`, and `linelen % oldmsgw != 0` at `tui.c:610` each leaves the suite green. They are not equivalent mutants — I reproduced visible differences by hand. The prompt `" Are you sure?"` is 14 characters (instrumented build: `linelen=14`), so exact fill needs a message window of 14 or 7 columns, i.e. a terminal of 16 or 9 columns. At 80x24→16x24 the `:554` mutant garbles the screen where the fixed build restores cleanly:

  ```
  fixed:   COMMAND> rest 5      mutant:   COMMAND> rest
           Are you sure?                  Are you sure? 5
           y                              y
  ```
  and dragging 16→12→9 shows the `:669` and `:610` mutants diverging too (instrumentation confirms `nl=0` and `pad=0` fire at those steps). All of it is below the documented 72-column minimum, which is #94's territory — so this is low-severity untested-but-live code, not a defect.

- **An ended line restored while a *pause* waits has no coverage.** Adding `if (pending_answer == NULL) return;` right after `ended = TRUE` leaves the whole suite green. That path is live: `pause(1)` in `sst.c:772-775` writes `[ANNOUNCEMENT ARRIVING...]` / `[IMPORTANT ANNOUNCEMENT ARRIVING -- HIT SPACE BAR TO CONTINUE]` with `prout` and then `getch()`, so `ended` is true and `pending_answer` is NULL. `tui.sh`'s existing resize-pause block uses the help pager, which is `proutn("[CONTINUE?]")` — a `curline` case, not this one. The gap predates this change (it arrived with #112), but the change rewrites how `want` is built for exactly that case, so nothing guards the rewrite.

## Reachability and comments in `restore_curline()`

Nothing became unreachable. Two comments now describe behavior the change removed, and both are unchanged from `main`:

- `tui.c:356` — `cursor_at_prompt`'s comment still says a prompt that ended its own line "was not kept -- see lastline, which covers most of those now, **and #117 for the case it does not**." There is no such case any more; what is left is a window too short, which the comment does not say.
- `tests/tui.sh:1371-1375` — the comment introducing the block you rewrote still reads "once the answer is part typed, the question is **left alone** -- #117 -- which has to be asserted as 'never more than one', **not as a restore**", directly above the assertion that now demands the restore. The inner comment at 1396 was updated; this outer one was not.

Two smaller notes, both about code the diff touched:

- Of the three exact-fill guards, only `tui.c:610` carries a note ("Guarded like the padding above"). `tui.c:554` and `tui.c:669` acquired the `% width != 0` condition with no comment, so the narrative that "three places are guarded" is only visible in one of them.
- `tui.c:502`'s `width > 0` conjunct can never be false — it sits inside `if (r >= 0 && width > 0)` at `tui.c:461`. Harmless, but it reads as a live guard.
- New `-Wshadow` warning (not in the project's flag set, so CI stays green): `int alen` at `tui.c:510` shadows `int alen` at `tui.c:473`. Same value in that branch, so not a bug.

## Documentation

- **CRLF:** all 25 added `sst.doc` lines end `\r\n`; none was added bare-LF.
- **Width:** maximum 70 columns excluding the CR — four lines land on exactly 70 (`whatever you had typed of an answer to it -- but look at both before`, `first word of your answer and only its first letter, so an "N" typed`, `characters. Where the terminal cannot grow, do not answer and do not`, `"N", never repeating what it wanted; answer N to decline whatever it`), the rest ≤69. If the rule is "under 70" those four are over by one; nothing in the repo enforces a width, the file's own maximum is 79, and the section already contained a 73. `git diff --check` flags every added line as trailing whitespace — that is the CR, and `sst.doc` is not listed in `.gitattributes`, so it happens on any edit to this file.
- **Manual vs game, measured.** Your residual numbers reproduce exactly at 72 columns with a 90-character answer: 72x17 and 72x16 restore both; 72x15 keeps the whole answer and loses the question; 72x14 leaves a 34-character fragment. Growing back one row at a time restores the answer at 15 and the question at 16 — so "give the terminal another row or two" and "the question comes back with your typing untouched" are both literally true.
- **Manual vs README:** they agree, and the paragraph at `README.md:16-21` that this change did *not* touch ("both the question you were asked and the answer you were halfway through typing survive, so long as there is still room for them") was an overclaim on `main` and becomes true with the fix.
- One accuracy point: `sst.doc:1591` says "the self-destruct password **is** nine characters". `setup.c:532` prompts "Please type in a secret password (9 characters maximum)-" and `sst.h:279` declares `passwd[10]`, so it is up to nine and the player chooses it. The argument the sentence is making (retyping is a nuisance) survives the correction.
- Pagination: the section's "page" grows 127→133 lines between form feeds, already by far the longest in the file (others 47-67) on `main`. No regression, and `help` and `instructions` both pass.

## Journey coverage I ran by hand

All against `./build-debug/sst`, each in tmux on its own `-L` socket with `-f /dev/null`, cleaned up with `kill-server` on that socket only.

- 13-step slow drag 80x24→72x20→80x24 with a one-character answer: exactly one question at every step, no stacking.
- Width drag 80→78→76→74→72→80 with the 90-character answer: one question per step, and the full 90 characters restored across two rows at the end. **No test covers this** — the new block drags height only, and the three-size block does one width step with a one-character answer. It passes, but nothing guards it.
- Small-window robustness, 90-character answer through 80x14, 80x13, 72x14, 72x24, 80x15, 80x24: never more than one question, no crash, no garbling, and on return the pair is whole. Then Ctrl-U → `n` → `COMMAND>`, then `quit` → score → play-again, so the game exits cleanly after the drag.
- The self-destruct prompt, a longer ended line (`SELF-DESTRUCT-SEQUENCE-WILL-BE-ABORTED` after `prout` at `finish.c:24`): typed `zz`, dragged 80x23 / 80x24 / 76x20 / 80x24 / 72x24 — prompt and answer each present exactly once at every step, and Enter then reaches `PASSWORD-REJECTED` and returns to `COMMAND>`.

## Environment issues

- **No `cppcheck`, `clang-tidy`, `scan-build`, or `valgrind` installed**, and no `clang`. The static pass was therefore compiler warnings only: the project's `-Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes` (clean), `-Werror` (clean), and an extra `-Wshadow -Wconversion -Wsign-conversion` run diffed against `main` (one new warning). `shellcheck` is present and clean. Treat the analyzer pass as not run, not as a pass.
- **gcov coverage of `restore_curline()` could not be collected.** A `--coverage` build run through `tests/tui.sh` produced a `tui.c.gcda` recording exactly one process — `make_windows` count 1, the whole of `restore_curline` `#####` — because the tmux sessions are torn down rather than exited, so the resizing processes never flush. Scripted clean-exit runs did not flush either. I substituted the mutation battery above and an `fprintf`-instrumented build (in a `/tmp` copy) for the branch-level questions.

## Reproducing

```sh
cmake -S . -B build-debug  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug   -DSST_WERROR=ON && cmake --build build-debug
cmake -S . -B build-release -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DSST_WERROR=ON && cmake --build build-release
ctest --test-dir build-debug --output-on-failure
ctest --test-dir build-release --output-on-failure
printf 'regular\nshort\nnovice\nxyz\nsrscan\nlrscan\nstatus\ndamages\nchart\nquit\nn\n' | ./build-debug/sst
```
